read.caption: WHO course DVD, disc 1. Complete a recording form as you watch. Videos are used to show signs: the classification discussed at the end of the video may not be accurate, because of recent technical updates.

read.text: What treatments are identified for Jacob?

stages.text: You have classified Jacob's problem as PNEUMONIA.
stages.question: Which treatments does the classification table identify?
options: An oral antibiotic, a safe remedy for the cough, and advice on when to return
Urgent referral with a first dose of antibiotic
A safe remedy only: no antibiotic
stages.explanation: An oral antibiotic; soothe the throat and relieve the cough with a safe remedy; and advise Amira when to return: in 3 days for PNEUMONIA, or immediately if he worsens.

stages.text: Jacob is able to drink, so you prescribe amoxicillin as syrup: 5 ml (250 mg/5 ml) twice a day for 5 days.
stages.question: Which soothing remedy is right for Jacob?
options: A cough syrup from the pharmacy
stages.explanation: Jacob is breastfed, so breast milk is an important remedy for him.

read.text: Practise

sections.title: Counsel the caregiver: giving medicine at home

read.text: Use good communication skills to teach a caregiver to give an oral medicine at home, and label the medicine.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Counselling the caregiver of a child with pneumonia
read.caption: Watch this first.

read.text: Counselling is an important opportunity to cover home treatment, feeding, care in the home, and when to return to the clinic. You counsel the caregiver after you have assessed, classified and decided on treatment for all conditions.

read.title: APAC: use it as you assess, classify, treat and counsel

cards.back: Find out what the child's problems are and what the caregiver is already doing for the child.
Praise the caregiver for what she has done well.
Advise her how to care for her child at home.
Check the caregiver's understanding, using checking questions.

steps.title: Give information
steps.text: Use words the caregiver understands, and focus on the most important messages.

steps.title: Show an example
steps.text: Use familiar objects as teaching aids.

steps.title: Let her practise
steps.text: Affirm, give feedback, and allow more practice as needed.

read.text: For cough or difficult breathing you counsel on: giving oral antibiotics at home, giving soothing remedies at home, how to use an inhaler if needed for wheezing, when to return immediately, and when to come for follow-up.
Giving oral medicines at home

Oral medicines are given for different reasons, in different doses and on different schedules, but the way to give each one is similar. If a caregiver learns how to give a medicine correctly, the child will be treated properly.

read.title: Teaching a caregiver to give an oral medicine

steps.title: Determine the medicine and the dose
steps.text: For the child's weight and age.

steps.title: Explain the treatment
steps.text: Tell the caregiver why you are giving the medicine to the child.

steps.title: Demonstrate
steps.text: Show how to measure a dose.

steps.title: Let her practise
steps.text: Watch her measure a dose by herself. Tell her what she has done correctly. If she measured it incorrectly, show her again.

steps.title: Ask her to give the first dose
steps.text: She gives it to the child in the clinic.

steps.title: Explain carefully, then label and package
steps.text: Tell her how much to give, how many times a day, when to give it (such as early morning, lunch, dinner, before going to bed) and for how many days. Write this on a drug label.

read.text: How do you label and package a medicine?

steps.title: Write the full name of the medicine
Write the total amount
steps.text: The tablets, capsules or syrup needed to complete the course of treatment.

steps.title: Write the daily dose and schedule
steps.text: For example: ½ tablet twice daily for 5 days. Write the dose (tablets, capsules, drops or spoonfuls) and when to give it.

steps.title: Package it
steps.text: Put the total amount of each medicine into its own labelled, clean container: an envelope, paper, tube or bottle. Then give it to the mother.

cards.back: Give, collect, count and package each medicine separately.
Explain that all the tablets or syrup must be used to finish the course of treatment, even if the child gets better.
Ask checking questions to make sure she understands how to treat her child. If a dispenser teaches the caregiver in your clinic, teach these skills to the dispenser.

read.text: A mother tells you that she already knows how to give the treatment. What should you do?
read.answer: Ask her to show you how to measure the dose, and to tell you the schedule for the antibiotic. If she is incorrect, give her the information and demonstrate. If she does know and measures the dose correctly, ask her to give the first dose so that you can observe.

sections.title: Counsel the caregiver: when to return, and counselling Amira

read.text: Tell a caregiver when to return for follow-up and when to return immediately, and ask good checking questions.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: When to return for follow-up

cards.back: Follow up in 3 days.

cards.front: A child with COUGH OR COLD
cards.back: Follow up in 5 days if not improving.

read.text: When to return immediately
Always counsel the caregiver on the signs that mean she should bring the child back to the clinic immediately.

cards.back: Is not able to drink or breastfeed; becomes sicker; develops a fever.

cards.front: A child with COUGH OR COLD
cards.back: Develops fast breathing or difficult breathing.

read.text: How will you counsel Amira about Jacob's pneumonia?

stages.text: You explain to Amira that Jacob is breathing faster than he normally should, and that you think he has pneumonia. Amira becomes very panicked and says that Jacob is going to die. She says she must run home with him in case he dies away from home and her husband is furious with her.
stages.question: What do you do?
options: Ask her to sit down, calm her, and ask why she is so afraid
Tell her not to be silly
Let her go, and give her the syrup quickly
stages.explanation: You ask Amira to sit down and you try to calm her. She says she is afraid because her other child died so young. You explain that pneumonia is an infection, but there is treatment for him to take, and that she can give it at home. You will teach her the steps.

stages.text: You emphasize that it is really important that Jacob receives the treatment: without it he could become very ill. You explain that the infection can be treated but it will take some time, and she will need to give Jacob the antibiotic regularly. You encourage Amira to discuss this with Jacob's father, to ask him to help with the treatment, and to bring him to the clinic if he has questions.

Jacob gets his first dose in the clinic. You show Amira how to measure the correct dose of the syrup, ask her to practise measuring it while you watch, and then ask her to give the first dose to Jacob. You praise her for doing a good job.
stages.question: Amira asks whether she can stop the syrup when Jacob looks better. What do you say?
options: She must give it twice a day for the full 5 days, even if Jacob gets better
She can stop when the cough has gone
She should keep the rest for the next time he is ill
stages.explanation: You give her the bottle and remind her to give it twice a day for the full 5 days, even if Jacob gets better before then. You label the syrup and give her the package.

stages.text: You praise her again for bringing in her sick child, and encourage her to continue breastfeeding: it is the best way to soothe her son if his throat is sore. You ask her to bring Jacob back in 3 days and record the date. Then you take her Mother's Card and review the signs for returning immediately. Amira still seems fearful, but agrees with the plan.

read.text: Practise

sections.title: Follow-up care for cough or difficult breathing

read.text: Reassess a child who returns after pneumonia and decide whether the child is improving, the same or worse.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Follow-up care for pneumonia
read.caption: Watch this first.

read.text: A child with PNEUMONIA should come back in 3 days. A child with COUGH OR COLD should come back in 5 days if not improving. During a follow-up visit you do two things.

steps.title: Assess for cough or difficult breathing again
ASK three questions
steps.text: Is the child breathing slower than on his first visit? Is there less fever? Is the child eating better?

steps.title: Decide
steps.text: Is the child's respiratory condition improving, the same or worsening?

steps.title: Reassess the child fully
steps.text: Use the IMNCI process, with a second recording form, to see whether there are any new problems.

read.text: What do you do at follow-up? Sort each finding.

items.text: The child has a general danger sign
Chest indrawing or breathing rate, fever and eating are the same
items.why: The child is not worse, but is not improving either.

items.text: The child is breathing slower, without chest indrawing, is eating better and has less fever
items.why: The child is improving. He may still cough, but most children who are improving no longer have fast breathing.

read.explanation: When the child is improving, tell the mother that the child should finish taking the 5 days of the antibiotic, and review with her why finishing the entire course matters.

read.text: If a child needs follow-up for more than one condition, the child should come at the earliest definite follow-up.
read.label: Remember

read.text: How will you provide follow-up care for Jacob?

stages.text: A few days later Amira comes back, and this time her husband is with her. She looks more relaxed. You welcome them and praise them for bringing Jacob back. Amira tells you that she has been giving the antibiotic regularly, and that Jacob seems better.
Jacob is coughing much less. His breathing rate is now 40 breaths per minute. Amira says he is eating better: he will take solid foods and is breastfeeding better.
stages.question: How is Jacob?
stages.explanation: He is breathing slower and eating better. You tell his parents that he is much better. They are relieved.

stages.text: You have decided that Jacob is improving.
stages.question: What do you tell Amira to do now?
options: Finish the full 5 days of the antibiotic
stages.explanation: You remind Amira that Jacob should finish taking the 5 days of the antibiotic, review with her why that matters, and again praise the parents for their good care of Jacob.

read.text: Practise

sections.title: Using this module in your clinic

read.text: Plan how you will practise these skills in your own clinic.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: How will you begin to apply what you have learned? In the coming days, focus on these key clinical skills, using your chart booklet and recording form. Practising will help you understand the clinical signs.

cards.back:
• Ask caregivers if their children have a cough or difficult breathing, and for how long. Explain difficult breathing if they do not understand.
  • Count the number of breaths in one minute. Decide if it is fast breathing.
  • Watch children's chest walls: in normal children the chest wall and abdomen move out when the child breathes in.
  • Identify chest indrawing: the lower chest wall moves in when the child breathes in.
  • Listen for the different noises of breathing: do you hear stridor or wheezing?

• Use your chart booklet to classify the signs you identify.
  • Record your classifications and the treatment on your recording form.

• Determine the appropriate treatment for a respiratory classification.
  • Determine the correct type and dose of antibiotic.
  • Determine the safe remedies in your area.

• Use the key communication skills (APAC and the three teaching steps).
  • Teach a caregiver how to give the antibiotic at home.
  • Teach a caregiver about making or buying and giving a safe remedy for sore throat or cough.
  • Counsel about when to return for follow-up and when to return immediately.

• Reassess the child's previous classification.
  • Determine how you will manage.

read.text: Remember to use your logbook

• Complete the logbook exercises for Module 3.
  • Record at least 2 cases on IMNCI recording forms.
  • Take notes if you experience anything difficult, confusing or interesting during these cases, to share with your study group and facilitator.
Test what you have learned in Module 3.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Before the module you answered six questions. Answer them again now, to see what you have learned. Then take the logbook test: you may use your chart booklet, but not the module.
Look back on what you learned, plan how you will use it, and tell us what you think. When you finish this lesson the module badge is yours.
read.label: In this lesson
Recap
read.text:
What you learned

  • Count breaths for a full minute in a calm child: 50 or more is fast from 2 up to 12 months, 40 or more from 12 months.
  • Any danger sign or stridor in a calm child: SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE.
  • Fast breathing or chest indrawing: PNEUMONIA, oral amoxicillin for 5 days, follow up in 3 days.

In your clinic this week, record in your logbook three children you see for cough or difficult breathing: what you found, how you classified them and what you did. Bring the logbook to your next supervision visit or course session.
read.label: Your logbook

read.title: Reflect
prompts: What is one thing you will do differently in your clinic after this module?
Which part was hardest for you? What will you practise again?
read.ratingText: How useful was this module for your work?

read.text: See what Module 4 covers and which part of the recording form it uses, then take the pre-test.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Diarrhoea is likely a very common problem in the children you see at your clinic. Diarrhoea can be serious, and can even lead to death.

In Module 2 you were told to come to this module to assess and classify diarrhoea in sick young infants. The process is similar for the young infant and the child. There are some important differences, which this module points out as "For the young infant".
read.label: Diarrhoea in the sick young infant

steps.title: For ALL sick children
steps.text: Ask the caregiver about the child's problems, check for general danger signs, and assess for cough or difficult breathing.

steps.title: Then ASK: does the child have diarrhoea?
steps.text: If NO, go on to the next main symptom. If YES, assess and classify the child using the colour-coded classification charts for dehydration and diarrhoea.

steps.title: Continue the assessment
steps.text: Assess the next main symptoms (next is fever), check for malnutrition and anaemia, check immunization status and other problems.

read.text: What you will be able to do

After you study this module, you will be able to:

  • Define the types of diarrhoea and the levels of dehydration
  • Recognize the clinical signs of dehydration
  • Assess diarrhoea in sick children
  • Assess dehydration in young infants and sick children
  • Classify diarrhoea and the severity of dehydration using the IMNCI charts
  • Give Plans A, B and C for dehydration
  • Counsel the caregiver about home treatment for diarrhoea and dehydration
Which part of the recording form is used in this module?

read.caption: The national recording form: diarrhoea

read.text: Before you begin
What do you know now about managing diarrhoea? Check quickly with five questions. After the module you will answer the same questions, and see what you have learned.
Start the visit of a child with diarrhoea: greet the caregiver, check for danger signs and ask about cough.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Diarrhoea
read.caption: Watch this first.

read.text: Consider a typical case that you might see in your practice. You will follow Mary and her mother Ana through the whole module.

stages.text: It is a busy afternoon in your clinic. A young mother comes into your clinic room, carrying a small girl. She says her daughter, Mary, has diarrhoea. You ask the mother's name, and she says Ana. Ana says that Mary usually eats porridge and milk, but that she has had bad diarrhoea in the past few days. Ana tried giving more porridge but Mary is still sick. Ana thought it was a bad stomach from spoiled milk, and that it would pass.

The diarrhoea has remained for several days now, and Mary looks unwell. Ana fears that Mary is getting worse, and feels guilty that she did not come sooner. Ana works in the mornings and lives some distance from the clinic, so she has little time in the day to bring Mary in. She is worried that her family will blame her for working and letting Mary get more and more sick.
stages.question: How do you greet Ana and begin?
options: Praise her for bringing Mary, and explain that you will check her and decide the best treatment
Tell her she should have come on the first day
Give ORS packets at once and send them home
stages.explanation: You praise Ana for bringing in her daughter. You tell her that diarrhoea can be a serious problem for young children, but that there are ways to help her daughter get better. You explain that you will check her condition and decide the best treatment. Ana seems relieved.

stages.text: You ask Mary's age. Ana tells you that she is 9 months old. You ask if there are other problems besides the diarrhoea. She says no. This is their first visit for this diarrhoea. You take Mary's weight, 8.2 kg, and her temperature, 37 °C.

You check for general danger signs. Ana tells you that Mary is able to drink milk and take porridge. She does not vomit. She has not had convulsions. Mary looks very tired in Ana's arms, but she watches you as you speak. When you reach out to take her hand, she grabs your finger.
stages.question: Does Mary have a general danger sign?
options: Yes: she is not able to drink
stages.explanation: Mary can drink, does not vomit everything, has had no convulsions, and is awake: she watches you and grabs your finger. She has no general danger signs.

stages.text: Next you ask about cough or difficult breathing. Ana says that Mary had a cough about 2 months ago, but it has cleared up. So you move to the next main symptom, diarrhoea. This is also the problem that Ana brought Mary for.

sections.title: What diarrhoea is, and its types

read.text: Define diarrhoea and its three types, and ask the two questions that tell you the type.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: What is diarrhoea?

Diarrhoea occurs when stools contain more water than normal, and are loose or watery. In many regions diarrhoea is defined as three or more loose or watery stools in a 24-hour period. Children between the ages of 6 months and 2 years often have diarrhoea. It is more common in settings of poor sanitation and hygiene, including a lack of safe drinking water.
Most diarrhoea that causes dehydration is loose or watery. Cholera is one example, though only a small proportion of all loose or watery diarrhoeas are due to cholera.

read.title: The types of diarrhoea in children

cards.back: An episode of diarrhoea that lasts less than 14 days. Acute watery diarrhoea causes dehydration and contributes to malnutrition. The death of a child with acute diarrhoea is usually due to dehydration.
Lasts 14 days or more. Up to 20% of episodes of diarrhoea become persistent. This often causes nutritional problems and contributes to death in children.

Diarrhoea with blood in the stool, with or without mucus. The most common cause is Shigella bacteria. Amoebic dysentery is not common in young children. A child may have both watery diarrhoea and dysentery.

read.text: A young infant has diarrhoea if the stools have changed from the usual pattern, and are many and watery: more water than faecal matter. The normally frequent or semi-solid stools of a breastfed baby are not diarrhoea.
read.label: For the young infant

read.text: ASK: does the child have diarrhoea?

Ask ALL caregivers if the child has diarrhoea. Use words for diarrhoea that the mother understands: you may need to explain it as loose, watery stools. If the answer is NO, ask about the next main symptom, fever. If YES, or if diarrhoea was the reason for coming, you assess in two parts: the type of diarrhoea, and the signs of dehydration.

read.title: Two questions tell you the type

steps.title: ASK: for how long?
steps.text: Diarrhoea which lasts 14 days or more is persistent diarrhoea. Give the mother time to answer. She may need time to recall the exact number of days.

steps.title: ASK: is there blood in the stool?
steps.text: Ask the mother if she has seen blood in the stools at any time during this episode of diarrhoea. Diarrhoea with blood in the stool is dysentery, and needs specific treatment.

read.text: Which type of diarrhoea? Sort each child.

items.text: Loose stools for 3 days, no blood
Watery stools for 16 days, no blood
Diarrhoea for 2 days, the mother saw blood yesterday
items.why: Blood in the stool at any time during this episode.

items.text: Loose stools for 13 days, no blood

read.caption: Chart booklet: diarrhoea (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

sections.title: Look for dehydration: condition, eyes and drinking

read.text: Explain what dehydration is, and look for three of its signs: general condition, sunken eyes and how the child drinks.
read.label: In this lesson
Before you start
read.text: Which of these is a sign of dehydration you can check without equipment?
feedback: Right. You need only your fingers and your eyes.
Temperature is for fever.
Breathing is for cough.

read.text: What is dehydration?

Diarrhoea can be a serious problem, and can even lead to death, if the child becomes dehydrated. Dehydration is when the child loses too much water and salt from the body. This causes a disturbance of electrolytes, which can affect vital organs.

A child who is dehydrated must be treated to help restore the balance of water and salt. Many cases of diarrhoea can be treated with Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS), a mixture of glucose and several salts. ORS and extra fluids can be used as home treatment to prevent dehydration. Low osmolarity ORS should be used to treat dehydration.

When a child becomes dehydrated, he is at first restless or irritable. As the body loses fluids, the eyes may look sunken, and the skin loses elasticity. If dehydration continues, the child becomes lethargic or unconscious.
read.label: Key point

read.text: LOOK at the child's general condition

cards.back: You checked this with the general danger signs. A lethargic or unconscious child has a general danger sign. Remember to use this sign again when you classify the child's diarrhoea.
The child is restless and irritable all the time, or every time he is touched and handled. A child who is calm when breastfeeding but restless and irritable again when he stops has the sign.

cards.front: Upset only because he is in the clinic
cards.back: Many children are upset just because they are in the clinic. Usually these children can be consoled and calmed. They do NOT have the sign restless and irritable.

read.text: Watch the infant's movement. Does he move on his own? Does the infant move only when stimulated, and then stop? Is the infant restless and irritable? The young infant chart does not test how well the infant drinks.
read.label: For the young infant

read.text: LOOK for sunken eyes
The eyes of a child who is dehydrated may look sunken. Decide if you think the eyes are sunken. Then ask the mother if she thinks her child's eyes look unusual. Her opinion can help you confirm.
In a severely malnourished child who is wasted, the eyes may always look sunken, even if the child is not dehydrated. Still use the sign to classify dehydration.

read.title: DVD exercise: assess sunken eyes
read.caption: WHO course DVD, disc 1. Six children: does each have sunken eyes? The video reviews the answers with you.

read.text: LOOK to see how the child drinks
Ask the mother to offer the child some water in a cup or spoon. Watch the child drink.

cards.back: The child is not able to suck or swallow when offered a drink. A child may not be able to drink because he is lethargic or unconscious.
The child is weak and cannot drink without help. He may be able to swallow only if fluid is put in his mouth.
It is clear that the child wants to drink. He reaches out for the cup or spoon when you offer water. When the water is taken away, he is unhappy because he wants to drink more.
A child who takes a drink only with encouragement and does not want to drink more does NOT have the sign drinking eagerly, thirsty.

read.text: Does the child have the sign? Sort each observation.

items.text: Cries when the nurse comes near, but calms in his mother's arms
items.why: He can be consoled: not restless and irritable.

items.text: Fusses every time he is touched, and again whenever he stops breastfeeding
Grabs the cup and cries when it is taken away
Takes a sip when coaxed, then turns away
Swallows only when water is put in his mouth with a spoon

sections.title: The skin pinch, and assessing Mary

read.text: Do the skin pinch correctly, read the result, and assess Mary for diarrhoea and dehydration.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: The skin pinch is an important test for dehydration. When a child is dehydrated, the skin loses elasticity.

read.title: How to do the skin pinch
read.caption: The five steps of the skin pinch, and what slowly and very slowly look like.

read.title: The skin pinch in five steps

steps.title: ASK the mother to lay the child flat
steps.text: The child lies flat on his back on the examining table, with his arms at his sides (not over his head) and his legs straight. Or the mother holds the child lying flat on her lap.

steps.title: USE your thumb and first finger
steps.text: Locate the area on the child's abdomen halfway between the umbilicus and the side of the abdomen. Do not use your fingertips, because this will cause pain. The fold of skin should be in a line up and down the child's body.

steps.title: PICK UP all the layers
steps.text: Pick up all the layers of skin and the tissue underneath them.

steps.title: HOLD for one second
steps.text: Hold the pinch for one second. Then release it.

steps.title: LOOK at how the skin goes back
steps.text: Very slowly, slowly, or immediately.

read.title: How does the skin pinch go back?

cards.back: Longer than 2 seconds.
Less than 2 seconds, but not immediately. If the skin stays up for even a brief time after you release it, decide that the skin pinch goes back slowly.
The skin goes back at once when you release it.

read.text: The skin pinch is not always an accurate sign. In a child with severe malnutrition, the skin may go back slowly even if the child is not dehydrated. In a child who is overweight or has oedema, the skin may go back immediately even if the child is dehydrated. You should still use the skin pinch to classify the child's dehydration.

read.title: DVD exercise: assess skin pinch
read.caption: WHO course DVD, disc 1. Five children: very slowly, slowly or immediately? The video reviews the answers with you.

read.title: Demonstration: assess and classify diarrhoea
read.caption: WHO course DVD, disc 1. All the steps of assessing diarrhoea, in a clinical setting.

stages.text: Ana has already reported that Mary has diarrhoea. You ask how many days she has had diarrhoea, and Ana tells you 3 days. You ask if there is blood in her daughter's stool, and she tells you no.
stages.question: What does this tell you about the type of diarrhoea?
stages.explanation: 3 days is less than 14 days, and there is no blood in the stool.

stages.text: Now you examine Mary's condition. She seems restless and irritable, especially when you touch her. You check for sunken eyes, and it appears that she has them. Ana agrees that her daughter's eyes look unusual. You offer Mary some water. She drinks eagerly.
You ask Ana to place Mary flat on her back on the examining table, with her arms at her sides and her legs straight. You pinch the skin of Mary's abdomen, and it goes back in 1 second.
stages.question: How does Mary's skin pinch go back?
stages.explanation: It did not go back at once, and it took less than 2 seconds: slowly. On the recording form you tick restless and irritable, sunken eyes, drinking eagerly and skin pinch slowly.

read.title: Look for signs of dehydration, with photographs

steps.title: Look at the eyes
steps.text: Are they sunken? Ask the mother if the eyes look unusual to her.

steps.title: Pinch the skin of the abdomen
steps.text: Halfway between the umbilicus and the side, with the fold up and down the body. Hold for one second, then release.

steps.title: Decide how the skin goes back
steps.text: Very slowly (longer than 2 seconds), slowly, or immediately.

read.text: Record the signs of two children with diarrhoea on the recording form.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Now practise with two children. Read each case, record the signs on the recording form, and classify. If you are not yet sure of the classification, do the next two lessons and then come back.
Which two questions do you ask every caregiver whose child has diarrhoea?
read.answer: For how long? Is there blood in the stool?

read.text: Which four things do you look at or feel to find dehydration in a child?
read.answer: The child's general condition (lethargic or unconscious; restless and irritable), sunken eyes, how the child drinks when offered fluid, and the skin pinch.

read.text: Classify a child with diarrhoea as severe, some or no dehydration, and name the action for each.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: The main symptom diarrhoea has more than one classification table. When classifying:

• ALL children with diarrhoea are classified for dehydration.
  • If the child has had diarrhoea for 14 days or more, also classify for persistent diarrhoea.
  • If the child has blood in the stool, also classify for dysentery.

read.caption: Chart booklet: classify dehydration (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

read.title: Dehydration: the three classifications
read.text: Open each card: the signs, then what to do. Pink first, then yellow, then green.

cards.label: SEVERE DEHYDRATION
cards.signs: Two of the following signs: Lethargic or unconscious Sunken eyes Not able to drink or drinking poorly Skin pinch goes back very slowly.
cards.treat: If child has no other severe classification: Give fluid for severe dehydration (Plan C); If child has another severe classification: Refer URGENTLY to hospital with mother giving frequent sips of ORS on the way; Advise the mother to continue breastfeeding; If child is 2 years or older and there is cholera in your area, give antibiotic for cholera

cards.label: SOME DEHYDRATION
cards.signs: Two of the following signs: Restless, irritable Sunken eyes Drinks eagerly, thirsty Skin pinch goes back slowly.
cards.treat: Give fluid for some dehydration (Plan B); Give Zinc; If child has a severe classification: Refer URGENTLY to hospital with mother giving frequent sips of ORS on the way; Advise the mother to continue breastfeeding; Advise mother when to return immediately

cards.label: NO DEHYDRATION
cards.signs: Not enough signs to classify as severe or some dehydration.
cards.treat: Give fluid and food to treat diarrhoea at home (Plan A); Give Zinc; Advise mother when to return immediately; Follow-up in 5 days if not improving

read.title: Classify dehydration
read.caption: Two signs in a row decide the classification.

cards.back: Two or more of these signs: lethargic or unconscious; sunken eyes; not able to drink or drinking poorly; skin pinch goes back very slowly. The child needs fluids quickly: Plan C.
Two or more of these signs: restless, irritable; sunken eyes; drinks eagerly, thirsty; skin pinch goes back slowly. The child needs fluid, zinc and food: Plan B.
Not enough signs to classify as some or severe dehydration. The child needs extra fluid, zinc and food to prevent dehydration: Plan A, at home.

read.text: If a child has one sign in the red (top) row and one sign in the yellow (middle) row, classify the child in the yellow row: SOME DEHYDRATION.
read.label: Key point

read.text: What are your actions?

• SEVERE DEHYDRATION: if the child has no other severe classification, give fluid for severe dehydration (Plan C). If the child also has another severe classification, refer URGENTLY to hospital with the mother giving frequent sips of ORS on the way. Advise the mother to continue breastfeeding. If the child is 2 years or older and there is cholera in your area, give an antibiotic for cholera.
  • SOME DEHYDRATION: give fluid, zinc and food for some dehydration (Plan B). Breastfed children continue breastfeeding. Other children receive their usual milk or some nutritious food after 4 hours of treatment with ORS. If the child also has a severe classification, refer URGENTLY with the mother giving frequent sips of ORS on the way. Advise when to return immediately. Follow up in 5 days if not improving.
  • NO DEHYDRATION: give fluid, zinc and food to treat diarrhoea at home (Plan A). Advise when to return immediately. Follow up in 5 days if not improving.

Sudan national booklet: For SEVERE DEHYDRATION the national booklet also gives zinc for 14 days, and names the cholera antibiotic: for a child 2 years or older, erythromycin 250 mg, 1 tablet 4 times daily for 3 days (second line: tetracycline). WHO module (page 17): says only "give antibiotic for cholera", and lists zinc under SOME and NO DEHYDRATION.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: The young infant is classified with fewer signs, because the chart does not test drinking. SEVERE DEHYDRATION: two of movement only when stimulated or no movement at all, sunken eyes, skin pinch goes back very slowly. SOME DEHYDRATION: two of restless and irritable, sunken eyes, skin pinch goes back slowly. Follow up in 2 days if not improving.
read.label: For the young infant

read.text: Classify each child's dehydration.

items.text: Lethargic, and the skin pinch goes back very slowly
items.why: Two signs in the red row.

items.text: Sunken eyes, and drinks eagerly
items.why: Two signs in the yellow row.

items.text: Drinks eagerly; no other sign
Drinking poorly, and restless and irritable
items.why: One red sign and one yellow sign: classify in the yellow row.

items.text: Not able to drink, and sunken eyes
items.why: Two signs in the red row.

read.text: Classify a child with diarrhoea for 14 days or more, and a child with blood in the stool, then classify Mary.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: After you classify dehydration, classify the child for persistent diarrhoea if the child has had diarrhoea for 14 days or more. Then classify for dysentery if there is blood in the stool.
Diarrhoea for 14 days or more
Health workers often mismanage persistent diarrhoea, so these instructions are important.

cards.back: Diarrhoea for 14 days or more AND some or severe dehydration. Treat the dehydration before referral, unless the child has another severe classification. Refer to hospital.
Diarrhoea for 14 days or more and NO signs of dehydration. Special feeding is the most important treatment. Give zinc for 14 days. Follow up in 5 days.

read.text: Why refer the child with SEVERE PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA? These children need special attention to help prevent loss of fluid. They may need a change in diet. They may also need laboratory tests to identify the cause of the diarrhoea. Treating dehydration in a child who has another severe disease can be difficult, so that child is treated in hospital.

read.caption: Chart booklet: diarrhoea for 14 days or more (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

read.title: Persistent diarrhoea and dysentery
read.text: Open each card: the signs, then what to do. Pink first, then yellow, then green.

cards.label: SEVERE PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA
cards.signs: Dehydration present.
cards.treat: Treat dehydration before referral unless the child has another severe classification; Refer to hospital

cards.label: PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA
cards.signs: No dehydration.
cards.treat: Advise the mother on feeding a child who has PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA; Give dose of Vitamin A; Follow-up in 5 days

cards.label: DYSENTERY
cards.signs: Blood in the stool.
cards.treat: Give an oral ciprofloxacin for 3 days; Follow-up in 3 days

read.text: Sudan national booklet: For PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA, give zinc for 14 days. WHO module (page 17): says "give multivitamins and minerals (including zinc) for 14 days".
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: Blood in the stool

If the child has diarrhoea and any blood in the stool, classify as DYSENTERY. A child with dysentery is treated for dehydration, and is given an antibiotic recommended for Shigella: ciprofloxacin for 3 days.

Finding the actual cause of dysentery requires a stool culture, and it can take at least 2 days to get the laboratory results. You assume Shigella is the cause because Shigella causes about 60% of the dysentery cases seen in clinics, and nearly all cases of life-threatening dysentery.

read.caption: Chart booklet: blood in the stool (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

read.text: Sudan national booklet: A child with DYSENTERY is followed up in 3 days, and also receives zinc for 14 days. WHO module (page 19): the classification table says "follow-up in 2 days", while the counselling and follow-up sections of the same module say 3 days.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

stages.text: Mary has had diarrhoea for 3 days, and there is no blood in the stool.
stages.question: Do you classify Mary for persistent diarrhoea or dysentery?
options: No: it is an acute episode with no blood
stages.explanation: Persistent diarrhoea lasts 14 days or more. Dysentery has blood in the stool. Every child with diarrhoea is still classified for dehydration.

stages.text: When you assessed Mary you found that she is restless and irritable, has sunken eyes, is eager to drink, and her skin pinch goes back slowly.
stages.question: How do you classify Mary's dehydration?
stages.explanation: Mary has two or more signs in the yellow row and none in the red row: SOME DEHYDRATION.

stages.text: You tell Ana that Mary has some dehydration. It is not serious enough to send her to the hospital. You can begin treatment at the clinic, and she can continue treatment at home. Ana looks relieved.

read.title: DVD exercise: case study Josh
read.caption: WHO course DVD, disc 1. Record Josh's signs on a recording form. Does he have a general danger sign? How do you classify his respiratory illness and his diarrhoea?

read.text: Practise
Classify dehydration, persistent diarrhoea and dysentery for four children, and find an error on a recording form.
read.label: In this lesson
Before you start
read.text: How many signs of a row do you need to classify dehydration?
feedback: One is not enough.
Right. Two signs of the pink row, or two of the yellow row.
Two are enough.

read.title: The skin pinch
read.text: Watch the skin pinch, then decide how it goes back.
read.given: Until this clip is recorded: after you let go, the skin stays up for about 3 seconds before it goes back.
read.question: How does the skin go back?
feedback: The skin stays up for a moment: it is not immediate.
Slowly means the skin stays up for a brief instant only.
Right. Longer than 2 seconds is very slowly, a sign of severe dehydration.

dialogue.text: Let us see if Hiba wants to drink. Can you give her some water from this cup?
Look, she grabs the cup and drinks fast!

stages.question: What sign is this?
stages.explanation: A child who reaches for the cup and drinks fast is thirsty: a yellow-row sign.
feedback: Right.
She is able to drink.
Drinking fast and wanting more is eager drinking.

dialogue.text: Is she very sick?
She is restless, her eyes are sunken, and she is thirsty. She has some dehydration.

stages.question: What do you do now?
options: Give ORS in the clinic (Plan B) and zinc
Send her home with Plan A
stages.explanation: SOME DEHYDRATION: give fluid, zinc supplements and food for some dehydration (Plan B).
feedback: Right.
Plan A is for no dehydration.
Hiba has no severe classification.

cases.text: Hiba has had diarrhoea for 3 days, with no blood. She is restless and irritable. Her eyes are sunken. When you offer her water, she drinks eagerly. The skin pinch goes back immediately.

record.title: Does the child have diarrhoea? Yes

cases.question: How do you classify Hiba's dehydration?
feedback: Hiba has none of the pink-row signs except sunken eyes. Two pink-row signs are needed.
Right. She has restless and irritable, sunken eyes and drinks eagerly: two or more signs of the yellow row.
Hiba has three signs of the yellow row, more than enough to classify SOME DEHYDRATION.
cases.explanation: Some dehydration: give fluid, zinc supplements and food for some dehydration (Plan B).

cases.text: Yousif has had watery diarrhoea for 2 days. He is lethargic. His eyes are sunken. When you offer water, he drinks poorly. The skin pinch goes back very slowly.

record.title: Does the child have diarrhoea? Yes
lines: Skin pinch: goes back very slowly

cases.question: How do you classify Yousif's dehydration?
feedback: Right. He has all four signs of the pink row; two are enough.
Start at the top row. Two pink-row signs classify SEVERE DEHYDRATION.
Yousif has every sign of severe dehydration.
cases.explanation: Lethargic is also a general danger sign. If the child has no other severe classification, give fluid for severe dehydration (Plan C).

cases.text: Rayan has had diarrhoea for 16 days, with no blood. He is alert, his eyes are not sunken, he drinks normally and the skin pinch goes back immediately.

record.title: Does the child have diarrhoea? Yes

cases.question: Which classifications does Rayan have for his diarrhoea? Select all that apply.
feedback: Severe persistent diarrhoea needs dehydration as well. Rayan has no dehydration.
Right. Diarrhoea for 14 days or more with no dehydration is PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA.
Right. Classify dehydration for every child with diarrhoea. Rayan has no signs, so NO DEHYDRATION.
There is no blood in the stool.
cases.explanation: A child with diarrhoea is classified for dehydration, and also for persistent diarrhoea if it has lasted 14 days or more, and for dysentery if there is blood in the stool.

cases.text: Nour has had diarrhoea for 5 days and her mother has seen blood in the stool. Nour is restless and irritable and her eyes are sunken. She drinks normally and the skin pinch goes back immediately.

record.title: Does the child have diarrhoea? Yes

cases.question: Which classifications does Nour have? Select all that apply.
feedback: Nour has only one pink-row sign (sunken eyes).
Right. Restless and irritable plus sunken eyes are two yellow-row signs.
She has two signs of the yellow row, so she is dehydrated.
Right. Blood in the stool classifies DYSENTERY.
cases.explanation: Nour needs Plan B, zinc, and an antibiotic for dysentery (oral ciprofloxacin for 3 days in the Sudan booklet).

read.title: Find the error on Huda's form
read.text: One entry on this form is wrong. Tap it.

record.title: Does the child have diarrhoea? Yes

lines.why: This sign is in the yellow row.
This sign is in both rows.

classify.why: Restless and irritable plus sunken eyes are two signs: SOME DEHYDRATION.

read.explanation: Two signs of the yellow row are enough to classify SOME DEHYDRATION.

sections.title: Treat: three fluid plans, and Plan C

read.text: Match each dehydration classification to its fluid plan, and decide how a severely dehydrated child gets Plan C.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Children with diarrhoea are treated for dehydration. They are also treated for their diarrhoea, if they have persistent diarrhoea or dysentery. The treatments in this module are all new: Plans A, B and C for giving fluids and food, ORS, zinc, and ciprofloxacin for dysentery.

read.title: Three plans to replace water and salts

cards.back: SEVERE DEHYDRATION. Urgent treatment: rehydrate quickly with intravenous (IV) fluids.
SOME DEHYDRATION. Treat at the clinic with low osmolarity ORS.
NO DEHYDRATION. Treat diarrhoea at home.

read.text: How is Plan C given?
Severely dehydrated children and young infants need to have water and salts quickly replaced. Plan C requires rapid hydration using IV fluids or a nasogastric (NG) tube.
Rehydration using IV fluids or a nasogastric tube is recommended ONLY for children who have SEVERE DEHYDRATION.
read.label: Key point

read.text: Where is Plan C given?

Plan C in your chart booklet is a flow chart for deciding the safest place to treat the severely dehydrated child. It depends on the equipment available at your clinic or at a nearby clinic or hospital, the training you have received, and whether the child can drink.

• If IV treatment is available within a 30-minute drive, refer URGENTLY to hospital for treatment with IV fluids. On the way, have the mother offer frequent sips of ORS to her sick child.
  • If you cannot give IV or NG fluid and the child cannot drink, refer the child URGENTLY to the nearest hospital that can give IV or NG treatment.

Plan C by IV in the national booklet: 100 ml/kg Ringer's lactate (or normal saline)

AgeFirst give 30 ml/kg inThen give 70 ml/kg in
Under 12 months1 hour5 hours
12 months up to 5 years30 minutes2½ hours

Repeat the first 30 ml/kg once if the radial pulse is still very weak. Reassess the child every 1 to 2 hours, and classify the dehydration again at the end (after 6 hours in an infant, 3 hours in a child).
The WHO module does not print the Plan C amounts: it asks you to open Plan C in your chart booklet. The amounts above are read from the Sudan national booklet.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: Are you able to give Plan C in your clinic? If not, where will you refer?
read.answer: Decide this now for your own clinic, before you need it. Check what equipment you have for IV fluid, whether you are trained to use a nasogastric tube for rehydration, and which facility within a 30-minute drive can give IV fluid.

read.text: A 2-year-old has SEVERE DEHYDRATION and no other severe classification. Your clinic cannot give IV fluid, but the hospital 20 minutes away can. He can drink. What do you do?
options: Refer URGENTLY for IV fluids, with his mother giving frequent sips of ORS on the way
Give Plan B for 4 hours, then reassess
Send him home on Plan A with 2 packets of ORS
read.explanation: IV treatment is available within 30 minutes, so refer urgently, with sips of ORS on the way.

sections.title: Treat: Plan B at the clinic

read.text: Decide the amount of ORS for the first 4 hours, show the mother how to give it, and reassess the child.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: A child or young infant with SOME DEHYDRATION needs fluid, zinc and food. Plan B begins with a 4-hour treatment period at the clinic. During the 4 hours, the mother slowly gives a recommended amount of ORS solution. If the child needs treatment for other problems, start treating the dehydration first. Then give the other treatments. Zinc is given just as in Plan A.

read.title: Plan B in the clinic
read.caption: Four hours of ORS, and what to do during them.

read.text: Step 1. Determine the amount of ORS for the first 4 hours

AgeWeightORS in the first 4 hours
Up to 4 monthsUnder 6 kg200–400 ml
4 months up to 12 months6 kg up to 10 kg400–700 ml
12 months up to 2 years10 kg up to 12 kg700–900 ml
2 years up to 5 years12 kg up to 19 kg900–1400 ml

Look below the child's weight. Use the age only if you do not know the weight. If you have no chart, multiply the child's weight in kg by 75: an 8 kg child needs 8 × 75 = 600 ml.

The child will usually want to drink as much as he needs. If the child wants more or less than the estimated amount, give him what he wants. The mother should also breastfeed whenever the baby wants to, then resume the ORS solution.

Sudan national booklet: The amounts above are those of the national booklet. WHO module (page 36): its worked example for a 9-month-old uses a range of 450 to 800 ml, but its own answer key for Exercise E uses the same ranges as the national booklet (for example 400 to 700 ml at 11 months).
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: Step 2. Show the mother how to give ORS solution

Find a comfortable place in the clinic for the mother to sit with her child. Tell her how much ORS solution to give over the next 4 hours, and show her the amount in units that are used in your area. If the child is less than 2 years, show her how to give a spoonful frequently. If the child is older, show her how to give frequent sips from a cup. Sit with her while she gives the first few sips. Ask her if she has any questions.

While the mother gives ORS for 4 hours

  • Show her where to wash her hands, and where she can change the child's nappy or the child can use a toilet.
  • Check with her from time to time to see if she has problems. If the child is not drinking the ORS solution well, try another method: a dropper, or a syringe without the needle.
  • Use the time to teach. The first concern is to rehydrate the child. When the child is obviously improving, the mother can turn her attention to learning how to mix and give ORS solution (Plan A).
  • It is a good idea to have printed information she can study while she sits with her child. Posters on the wall reinforce it.

During the first 4 hours, encourage the mother to pause to breastfeed whenever the infant wants, then resume giving ORS. Give a young infant who does not breastfeed an additional 100–200 ml of clean water during this period.
read.label: For the young infant

read.text: Step 3. Reassess after 4 hours

read.title: After 4 hours, classify the dehydration again

cards.back: Move to Plan A. Counsel on home care.
Choose Plan B again. Begin feeding the child in the clinic: offer food, milk or juice. Continue to breastfeed frequently if the child is breastfed.
Begin Plan C.

A sign of overhydration. It is not a danger sign. The child has been rehydrated and does not need more ORS solution at this time. Give clean water or breast milk, and ORS according to Plan A when the puffiness is gone.

read.text: If the child is not taking the ORS solution, or seems to be getting worse, reassess before the four hours are over.

read.title: If the caregiver must leave before the 4 hours are finished

steps.title: Show her how to prepare ORS solution
steps.text: Have her practise.

steps.title: Show her how much ORS to give
steps.text: Enough to complete the 4-hour treatment at home.

steps.title: Give her packets
steps.text: Enough to complete rehydration, PLUS 2 more packets as recommended in Plan A.

steps.title: Explain the 4 rules of home treatment
steps.text: Extra fluid, zinc, continue feeding, when to return.

read.text: A child who has SOME DEHYDRATION and a severe classification needs urgent referral. Do not try to rehydrate the child before he leaves. Quickly give the mother some ORS solution and show her how to give frequent sips on the way. The exception is SEVERE PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA: this child is rehydrated first, then referred.
read.label: Key point

stages.text: Mary has SOME DEHYDRATION, so she needs Plan B: fluid, food and zinc. Mary is 9 months old and weighs 8.2 kg.
stages.question: How much ORS should Mary receive in the first 4 hours?
stages.explanation: By weight (6 kg up to 10 kg) and by age (4 months up to 12 months) the chart gives 400–700 ml. By the second method, 8.2 kg × 75 is about 615 ml, which is within the chart range.

stages.text: You explain to Ana that Mary has diarrhoea with some dehydration and needs fluids and food. You ask her to stay at the clinic to give Mary ORS, and you show her how much to give from a cup. You take her to a corner where she can sit with Mary. You show her where she can wash her hands and change Mary or use the toilets. Ana is worried about staying too late, because her husband will worry. You assure her that she can give all of the ORS now, and that you will then decide together about treatment at home. Ana props Mary on her lap and slowly begins to give ORS from a cup. You also encourage her to breastfeed if Mary wants to.
After 4 hours, you reassess Mary. She has NO DEHYDRATION. Her diarrhoea continues.
stages.question: What now?
options: Plan A at home, with zinc and food
stages.explanation: Mary is ready to go home on Plan A. Plan A also includes giving zinc and food.

sections.title: Treat: Plan A and extra fluid at home

read.text: Name the four rules of home treatment, teach a caregiver to mix and give ORS, and say how much to give.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: A child with diarrhoea but NO DEHYDRATION needs fluid, zinc and food to prevent dehydration. This child can be treated at home with Plan A. Plan A depends on your teaching and advising skills, because you counsel the mother about the four rules of home treatment.

Eventually ALL children with diarrhoea need Plan A. A child with NO DEHYDRATION is put on Plan A right away. A child with more serious dehydration is first treated with Plan B or C, and then put on Plan A.
read.label: Key point

steps.title: 1. Give extra fluid
steps.text: As much as the child will take.

steps.title: 2. Give zinc
steps.text: Once a day for 14 days.

steps.title: 4. When to return
steps.text: For a follow-up visit, or immediately if danger signs develop.

read.text: Rule 1: give extra fluid

Tell the caregiver to give as much fluid as the child will take. The purpose is to replace the fluid lost in diarrhoea and so prevent dehydration. The critical action is to give more fluid than usual, as soon as the diarrhoea starts.

cards.back: Continue breastfeeding, and add ORS and clean water.
Breastfeed more frequently than usual. A breastfed child under 4 months is first offered a breastfeed, then given ORS.
ORS solution, food-based fluids (soup, rice water, yoghurt drinks) and clean water.

If the infant is exclusively breastfed, do not introduce a food-based fluid. If ORS will be given at home, show how much to give after each loose stool. The mother first offers a breastfeed, then gives ORS.

read.title: Mixing and giving ORS
read.caption: Teach the caregiver, then watch her do it.

steps.title: Wash your hands
steps.text: With soap and water.

steps.title: Pour all the powder from one packet into a clean container
steps.text: Use any available container, such as a jar, bowl or bottle.

steps.title: Measure 1 litre of clean water
steps.text: Or the correct amount for the packet used. It is best to boil and cool the water. If this is not possible, use the cleanest drinking water available.

steps.title: Pour the water into the container
steps.text: Mix well until the powder is completely dissolved.

steps.title: Taste the solution
steps.text: So you know how it tastes.

read.text: The caregiver should mix fresh ORS every day, in a clean container, and keep the container covered. She should throw away any solution remaining from the day before.
read.label: Remember

read.text: How much ORS at home?

Give the caregiver 2 packets of ORS to use at home. Show her how much fluid to give in addition to the usual fluid intake:

  • Up to 2 years: 50–100 ml after each loose stool
  • 2 years or older: 100–200 ml after each loose stool

Then tell her how to give it:

  1. Give frequent small sips from a cup.
  2. If the child vomits, wait 10 minutes. Then continue, but more slowly.
  3. Continue giving extra fluid until the diarrhoea stops.
For which children with NO DEHYDRATION is it especially important to give ORS at home?
read.answer: A child who was treated with Plan B or C during this visit: the child has just been rehydrated and needs ORS to stop dehydration coming back. And a child who cannot return to the clinic if the diarrhoea gets worse: for example, the family lives far away or the mother has a job she cannot leave.

read.text: How much ORS after each loose stool?

items.text: Kala, 6 months
Sam, 2 years
Kara, 15 months
Lalita, 4 years

sections.title: Treat: zinc, feeding and when to return

read.text: Give the right dose of zinc, advise the caregiver to continue feeding, and teach the signs to return immediately.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Rule 2: give zinc

Zinc treatment can considerably reduce the duration and severity of a child's episode of diarrhoea. It is also shown to decrease stool output, and to decrease the need to hospitalize a child with diarrhoea.
Zinc is only given to children 2 months up to 5 years.
read.label: Key point

read.text:
AgeZinc, once a day for 14 days
2 months up to 6 months½ tablet (20 mg tablet), or 5 ml syrup (10 mg/5 ml)
6 months or older1 tablet (20 mg), or 10 ml syrup
Sudan national booklet: The national booklet gives zinc as a 20 mg tablet or as syrup (10 mg per 5 ml). WHO module (page 31): gives the tablet only.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.title: Show the caregiver how to give zinc

cards.back: Dissolve the tablet in a small amount of expressed breast milk, ORS or clean water, in a small cup or spoon.
The tablet can be chewed, or dissolved in a small amount of clean water in a cup or spoon.
The mother gives her child the first zinc supplement in the clinic, while you watch.
Remind the caregiver to give zinc for the full 14 days, even after the diarrhoea has stopped.

read.text: Rule 3: continue feeding
The caregiver should continue feeding the child during the diarrhoea. A child with persistent diarrhoea has special feeding needs, which you will learn in the next lesson.
Rule 4: when to return

Tell the mother of ANY sick child to return immediately if the child:

  • Is not able to drink or breastfeed
  • Becomes sicker
  • Develops a fever

If the child has diarrhoea, also tell her to return if the child has:

  • Blood in the stool
  • Drinking poorly (this also includes not able to drink or breastfeed)
How much zinc each day? Sort each child with diarrhoea.

items.text: 4 months, 7.3 kg, SOME DEHYDRATION
37 months, 12 kg, NO DEHYDRATION
9 months, DYSENTERY
5 weeks old, NO DEHYDRATION
items.why: Zinc is only given from 2 months up to 5 years.

read.text: Give special feeding advice for persistent diarrhoea, treat dysentery, and say when an antibiotic is needed for diarrhoea.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: SEVERE PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA

These children have had diarrhoea for 14 days or longer and have signs of dehydration. They should be referred to hospital. They need special attention to prevent fluid loss. Treat the dehydration before referral, unless the child has another severe classification.
PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA

These children have had diarrhoea for 14 days or longer and have no signs of dehydration. Special feeding is the most important treatment. Children with persistent diarrhoea may have difficulty digesting milk other than breast milk. They need to temporarily reduce the amount of other milk in their diet.

read.title: Feeding advice for a child with PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA

cards.back: Give more frequent, longer breastfeeds, day and night.
Replace it with increased breastfeeding, OR replace it with fermented milk products such as yoghurt, OR replace half the milk with nutrient-rich semi-solid food.
Follow the feeding recommendations for the child's age. Give small, frequent meals (at least 6 times a day), and avoid very sweet foods or drinks.
Give zinc for 14 days. Follow up in 5 days.

read.text: DYSENTERY

Children with dysentery receive ciprofloxacin for 3 days, and zinc given in the same way as in Plans A and B. Treat dehydration as classified. Teach the caregiver to give the oral medicine at home, as you learned in the module on cough or difficult breathing.

Ciprofloxacin (250 mg tablet), twice daily for 3 days

AgeWeightEach dose
2 months up to 4 months4 kg up to 6 kg¼ tablet
4 months up to 12 months6 kg up to 10 kg½ tablet
12 months up to 5 years10 kg up to 19 kg1 tablet

Sudan national booklet: The dose is given in 250 mg tablets, and the child with DYSENTERY returns for follow-up in 3 days. WHO module (page 34): the answer key for Exercise G gives the dose as ciprofloxacin syrup (250 mg/5 ml), and the treatment section says follow-up in 2 days while the counselling and follow-up sections say 3 days.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: When should antibiotics be used for diarrhoea?

Antibiotics are not effective in treating most diarrhoea. They rarely help, and they make some children sicker. Unnecessary use of antibiotics may increase the resistance of some pathogens. Antibiotics are also costly, and money is often wasted on ineffective treatment. Therefore, do not give antibiotics routinely.
The only types of diarrhoea that should be treated with antibiotics are DYSENTERY, and SEVERE DEHYDRATION with cholera in the area.
read.label: Key point

read.text: Does this child need an antibiotic for the diarrhoea?

items.text: Watery diarrhoea for 3 days, NO DEHYDRATION
Blood in the stool for 2 days
Diarrhoea for 3 weeks, no dehydration, no blood
items.why: PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA: special feeding and zinc.

items.text: 3 years old, SEVERE DEHYDRATION, cholera in the area
items.why: A child of 2 years or older gets the antibiotic for cholera.

items.text: SOME DEHYDRATION after 2 days of watery stools

sections.title: Counsel the caregiver: the four rules

read.text: Counsel a caregiver on each of the four rules of home treatment, and check that she has understood.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Good teaching and advising skills are particularly important when treating dehydration and diarrhoea. The caregiver gives many of the treatments, in the clinic or at home, so you must teach her how. Every child with diarrhoea goes home on Plan A in the end, so every caregiver needs the four rules.

steps.title: Rule 1. Give extra fluid
steps.text: Tell the caregiver that during illness a child loses fluid due to fever, fast breathing or diarrhoea. The child will feel better and stay stronger if he drinks extra fluid. First, tell her to give as much fluid as the child will take, as soon as the diarrhoea starts. Second, teach her how to mix and give ORS, and ask her to practise as you observe.

steps.title: Rule 2. Give zinc
steps.text: Show the mother how to give the zinc. She gives the first dose in the clinic. Explain that she will continue for 14 days. Check her understanding with checking questions, and solve any problems she has.

steps.title: Rule 3. Continue feeding
steps.text: For a child with persistent diarrhoea, explain that other milk is temporarily reduced, and that the child must take more breast milk or other foods to make up for it. The child is seen again in 5 days, and gets further feeding instructions then.

steps.title: Rule 4. When to return
steps.text: Immediately if the child is not able to breastfeed or drink, becomes sicker, develops a fever or has blood in the stool. In 3 days if the child has dysentery. In 5 days if the child has persistent diarrhoea.

read.title: Extra fluid can be given by

cards.back: More frequently, and for longer feeds. If the child is exclusively breastfed, also give ORS or clean water.

cards.front: If the child is not breastfed
cards.back: Food-based fluids (soup, rice water, yoghurt drinks), or ORS.
Especially important if the child was treated on Plan B or C, or cannot return to the clinic if the diarrhoea gets worse.

read.text: If the child must come back for more than one illness, tell the caregiver the earliest definite date to return.
read.label: Remember

read.text: Which of these is the best checking question after you advise a mother about increasing fluids during diarrhoea?
options: How much fluid will you give your child?
Do you remember some good fluids to give your child?
Will you be sure to give your child extra fluid?
read.explanation: A good checking question cannot be answered with yes or no. It shows you what the caregiver has learned.

stages.text: After 4 hours of ORS, Mary has NO DEHYDRATION. You will now counsel Ana on Plan A. You give Ana a Mother's Card to take home. It reminds her of what fluids and food to give her child.

Rule 1. You tell Ana to give extra fluid, as much as Mary will take: breast milk, clean water, ORS, or food-based fluids such as soup, rice water and yoghurt drinks. Ana says that Mary takes rice water well, and she will still breastfeed. She will also try to get some yoghurt from a neighbour. You remind her to breastfeed as often as Mary will.
stages.question: You taught Ana to make ORS in the clinic. How do you check that she remembers?
options: "How much clean water do you need for 1 packet of ORS?"
"Do you remember how to make the ORS?"
"You will mix it with 1 litre of water, won't you?"
stages.explanation: Ana says, "1 litre." You also ask, "How will you give the ORS?" and she says, "With a cup, as she sits in my lap." You ask how often she will give it, and what she will do if Mary vomits. You remind her to wait 10 minutes, then continue more slowly. You give Ana 2 packets of ORS to take home.

stages.text: Rule 2. You advise Ana how to give Mary zinc.
stages.question: Mary is 9 months old. How much zinc will she take?
options: ½ tablet a day for 14 days
stages.explanation: A child of 6 months or older takes 1 full tablet (20 mg) a day for 14 days. You show Ana how to dissolve the tablet in a spoon with breast milk or clean water. You explain that zinc is a good nutrient for the body that will help with Mary's diarrhoea.

stages.text: Rule 3. You advise Ana to continue feeding Mary.
stages.question: How much ORS should Mary get after each loose stool?
stages.explanation: Mary is under 2 years: 50–100 ml after each loose stool.

stages.text: Rule 4. You advise Ana to return immediately if Mary is not able to breastfeed or drink, becomes sicker, develops a fever, or has blood in the stool. You use the Mother's Card to show these signs. Mary has no other illness that needs a follow-up date. Your checking questions showed how much Ana understands, and gave her a chance to ask questions. You feel confident that she understands home treatment, and you say goodbye to her and Mary.

read.text: Follow up a young infant with diarrhoea, a child with persistent diarrhoea and a child with dysentery.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: At a follow-up visit you first reassess the earlier classification: is the child improving, the same, or worsening? Then you reassess the child with the full IMNCI assessment to see if there are any new problems. You use a second recording form for this visit.
Diarrhoea in the sick young infant (follow-up in 2 days)
ASK: has the diarrhoea stopped?

cards.back: Tell the mother to continue exclusive breastfeeding. If the infant's signs are improving, tell her to continue giving the infant fluids and breastfeeding according to Plan A.

Reassess the young infant for diarrhoea. Classify the dehydration and select a fluid plan. If the signs are the same or worse, refer the infant to hospital. If the young infant has developed fever, give intramuscular antibiotics before referral, as for VERY SEVERE DISEASE.

read.text: Persistent diarrhoea (follow-up in 5 days)
ASK: has the diarrhoea stopped? How many loose stools is the child having per day?

cards.front: The diarrhoea has stopped (fewer than 3 loose stools a day)
cards.back: Tell the mother to follow the usual feeding recommendations for the child's age. If the child is not normally fed in this way, teach her the feeding recommendations on the COUNSEL chart.

cards.front: The diarrhoea has not stopped (3 or more loose stools a day)
cards.back: Do a full reassessment of the child. Identify and manage any problems that need immediate attention, such as dehydration. Then refer the child to hospital.

read.text: Dysentery (follow-up in 3 days)
ASK: are there fewer stools? Is there less blood in the stool? Is there less fever? Is there less abdominal pain? Is the child eating better?

cards.front: Fewer stools, less blood, less fever, less abdominal pain, and eating better
cards.back: The child is improving on ciprofloxacin. Usually all of these signs diminish if the antibiotic is working. If only some have diminished, use your judgment. Tell the mother to finish the 3 days of ciprofloxacin, and review why finishing the antibiotic is important.
Classify the dehydration with the classification table. Select the appropriate fluid plan and treat the dehydration.

cards.front: Stools, blood, fever, abdominal pain or eating are the same or worse
cards.back: The child is not improving: resistance of Shigella to the antibiotic may be the cause. Stop the first antibiotic and give the second-line antibiotic recommended for Shigella for 5 days. Give the first dose in the clinic, teach the caregiver how and when to give it, and advise her to return in 2 days.

read.text: REFER the child with dysentery who is not improving if he is less than 12 months old, OR was dehydrated on the first visit, OR had measles within the last 3 months.
read.label: Key point

read.text: If the child has received the second-line antibiotic for two days and has not improved, the child may have amoebiasis. This child may be treated with metronidazole, if it is available or can be obtained by the family, or referred for treatment. Amoebiasis can only be diagnosed with certainty when trophozoites of E. histolytica containing red blood cells are seen in a fresh stool sample.

stages.text: Mary had SOME DEHYDRATION and received Plan B in the clinic. You reassessed her, classified NO DEHYDRATION, counselled Ana on Plan A, and sent them home.
stages.question: When was Mary supposed to return?
options: Immediately if a sign to return appears, or in 5 days if she is not improving
Every day until the diarrhoea stops
stages.explanation: Ana and Mary were to return only if Mary's dehydration and diarrhoea did not improve. Mary does not return, and you are pleased: you hope it means that the fluid plan worked, and that Mary is no longer dehydrated or unwell.

sections.title: Using this module in your clinic

read.text: Plan how you will practise these skills in your own clinic.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: How will you begin to apply what you have learned about managing children with diarrhoea? In the coming days, focus on these key clinical skills. Practising them in your clinic, with your chart booklet and recording form, will help you observe and understand the signs you need to assess and classify a child with dehydration and diarrhoea.

cards.back:
• Assess children for diarrhoea: how long has the diarrhoea lasted? Is there blood in the stool?
  • Assess children for signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, the skin pinch, the child's condition, and the child's willingness and ability to drink.
  • Practise the skin pinch, and decide if it goes back very slowly, slowly or immediately.
  • Practise observing children's condition (restless, irritable, unconscious, lethargic) and willingness to drink.

• Use your chart booklet to classify the signs of dehydration.
  • Classify whether a child has persistent diarrhoea or dysentery.

• Determine if children need Plan A, B or C.
  • Determine how you will give Plan C in your facility: what equipment do you have for intravenous fluid? Is there a facility within a 30-minute drive that can give this fluid? Are you trained to use nasogastric tubes for rehydration?
  • Advise a caregiver on giving Plan B in your facility. Determine the correct amount of ORS.
  • Advise a caregiver about giving Plan A. Focus on the 4 rules of home treatment.

• Teach a caregiver how to make and give ORS. Determine the amounts required.
  • Advise a caregiver on giving extra fluid and continuing to breastfeed at home.
  • Advise a caregiver on giving zinc, show how to give the tablets, and say how often zinc should be given.
  • Advise a caregiver on continued feeding, especially for children with persistent diarrhoea.
  • Counsel a caregiver about when to return for follow-up, and when to return immediately.

read.text: Before your next clinic day: where will a child with SEVERE DEHYDRATION get Plan C?
read.answer: Write down your answer for your own clinic: can you give IV fluid or use a nasogastric tube? If not, which facility within a 30-minute drive can give IV fluid?

read.text: Remember to use your logbook

• Complete the logbook exercises for Module 4.
  • Record at least 2 cases on IMNCI recording forms.
  • Take notes if you experience anything difficult, confusing or interesting during these cases, to share with your study group and facilitator.
Test what you have learned in Module 4.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Before the module you answered five questions. Answer them again now, to see what you have learned. Then take the logbook test: you may use your chart booklet, but not the module.
Look back on what you learned, plan how you will use it, and tell us what you think. When you finish this lesson the module badge is yours.
read.label: In this lesson
Recap
read.text:
What you learned

  • Two signs of a row classify dehydration: pink is severe, yellow is some.
  • Plan C for severe, Plan B for some, Plan A for no dehydration; zinc for 14 days.
  • 14 days or more is persistent diarrhoea; blood in the stool is dysentery.

In your clinic this week, record in your logbook three children you see for diarrhoea: what you found, how you classified them and what you did. Bring the logbook to your next supervision visit or course session.
read.label: Your logbook

read.title: Reflect
prompts: What is one thing you will do differently in your clinic after this module?
Which part was hardest for you? What will you practise again?
read.ratingText: How useful was this module for your work?

read.text: See what Module 5 covers and which part of the recording form it uses, then take the pre-test.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: A fever can have many causes. Fever can be the only sign of a sick child, or it may be combined with other problems. It is important to keep the big picture in mind as you manage the child with fever. You will have to do a careful assessment to determine how serious the problem is. This module teaches you how to do this assessment.

steps.title: For ALL sick children
steps.text: Ask the caregiver about the child's problems, check for general danger signs, assess for cough or difficult breathing, and assess diarrhoea and dehydration.

steps.title: Then DETERMINE: does the child have fever?
steps.text: If NO, go on to the next main symptom. If YES, assess and classify the child using the colour-coded classification charts for fever.

steps.title: Continue the assessment
steps.text: Assess the next main symptom (ear problem), check for malnutrition and anaemia, check immunization status and other problems.

read.text: What you will be able to do

After you study this module, you will be able to:

  • Determine if a child has fever by measuring temperature, by history, or by feeling
  • Decide when to do a malaria test
  • Recognize the clinical signs of very severe febrile disease
  • Identify the clinical signs of measles and of complications from measles
  • Classify fever using the IMNCI charts
  • Classify measles and measles with complications
  • Give oral antimalarials
  • Give appropriate treatments for measles
  • Counsel on home treatment and follow-up care for children with fever
  • Provide follow-up care to children with fever
Which part of the recording form is used in this module?

read.caption: The national recording form: fever and measles

read.text: Before you begin
What do you know now about managing fever? Check quickly with five questions. After the module you will answer the same questions, and see what you have learned.
Start the visit of a child who feels hot: greet the caregiver, check for danger signs, and assess cough and diarrhoea first.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Fever
read.caption: Watch this first.

read.text: Consider a typical case that you might see in your practice. You will follow Sami and his mother Miriam through the whole module.

stages.text: It is a hot day in your clinic, and the waiting room is crowded with mothers. Miriam comes in with her son, Sami. He has been complaining of being "hot" for a few days, she says. Sami sits next to Miriam but does not look very energetic. When you ask him how he is feeling, he puts his head into his mother's skirt. He lies on her lap and looks unwell. You are not yet sure if he is unwell because of the heat, or if he has a fever.

You praise Miriam for bringing Sami to the clinic: she has listened to her son's complaints and brought him in. She tells you Sami is 3 years old. She says he handles the heat well, and that his body feels warm. She has put cool, wet rags on his chest and head, but they have not helped. This is her first visit for this problem. You take Sami's temperature under his armpit: 38.6 °C. He weighs 12 kg.
stages.question: Does Sami have fever?
options: Yes: his axillary temperature is 37.5 °C or above
No: it is a hot day
You cannot tell without a blood test
stages.explanation: A child has fever if he has a history of fever, feels hot, or has an axillary temperature of 37.5 °C or above.

stages.text: You check for general danger signs. Miriam says Sami is able to eat and drink. He is not vomiting, and has not had convulsions. Sami acts very tired and keeps his head on his mother's lap, but he watches you as you talk. He holds the material of Miriam's skirt and plays with it.
stages.question: Does Sami have a general danger sign?
options: Yes: he is not able to drink
stages.explanation: Sami can drink, does not vomit everything, has had no convulsions, and is awake and watching you.

stages.text: You ask about cough: Miriam says no. You ask about diarrhoea: she says Sami has had loose stools for the last week, with no blood. Sami is not restless or irritable. His eyes are not sunken. He is shy to take a glass of water, but then drinks eagerly. His skin pinch goes back immediately.
stages.question: How do you classify Sami's diarrhoea?
stages.explanation: Sami has only one sign (drinks eagerly), so NO DEHYDRATION: you will counsel Miriam on Plan A. One week is less than 14 days, and there is no blood, so no persistent diarrhoea and no dysentery.

stages.text: Now you will assess Sami for the next main symptom, fever. This was his complaint, and you have already found by taking his temperature that he has a fever.

sections.title: What causes fever: malaria, measles and more

read.text: Say when a child has the main symptom fever, and name its common and dangerous causes.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: When does a child have the main symptom fever?

• The child has a history of fever, OR
  • The child feels hot, OR
  • The child has an axillary (underarm) temperature of 37.5 °C or above (38 °C rectal)

A child with fever may have malaria, measles or another severe disease, like meningitis, septicaemia or very severe pneumonia. Signs of some very severe diseases may be general and non-specific. It is very important to identify the key signs of the diseases that may cause the child's death very quickly: all sick children with those signs are referred to hospital.

Other bacterial infections causing fever include pneumonia, acute ear infection, streptococcal sore throat, dysentery, local bacterial infection, typhoid and urinary tract infection. Or a child with fever may have a simple cough or cold or another viral infection.
