read.title: Where national policy is breastfeeding with ARVs

cards.back: Feed like any other child: exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, complementary foods from 6 months, and breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond.

Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, complementary foods from 6 months, breastfeeding for the first 12 months, then stop only once a nutritionally adequate and safe diet without breast milk is possible.
Breastfeeding may still give the infant a greater chance of HIV-free survival, for example in emergencies.

read.text: At follow-up of a mother who breastfeeds, what do you check?
read.answer: That she breastfeeds exclusively with no other milk, water or food; often and as long as the baby wants; any feeding problem (not enough milk, crying, sore nipples); a breastfeed and her breasts if needed; that she is on ART or ARV prophylaxis and adheres; and her health, with a CD4 count in the last 6 months.

read.text: At follow-up of a formula-fed infant, what do you check?
read.answer: Only replacement feeds, never breast milk or unsafe fluids; the right volume and number of feeds; correct measuring; clean preparation (boiled and cooled); fresh feeds each time; cup feeding; cup and utensils cleaned in hot soapy water. Ask the caregiver to show you, and demonstrate if needed.

read.text: WHO (2016) now recommends that mothers living with HIV breastfeed for at least 12 months and may continue up to 24 months or beyond, fully supported with ART. Follow the current national recommendation.
read.label: Changed since 2014

read.text: Advise on feeding an HIV-infected child with special problems, and help a mother stop breastfeeding safely.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text: Infections like TB and diarrhoea cause loss of appetite, weight loss and acute malnutrition in HIV-infected children. Always advise the mother to continue feeding and giving fluids during illness, and to feed more after it.

cards.back: Treat it. Breastfeed at least 8 times in 24 hours; give small meals at least 5 times a day, with added oil or nuts.
Treat it, feed as above, deworm and give vitamin A if not given in the last 6 months.
Treat the thrush. Give mashed or pureed food, no spicy food; paracetamol half an hour before feeds may help in extreme cases.
Give small frequent sips and food the child likes, let the child eat before the medicine; for ritonavir, coat the tongue with peanut butter first.
Soft, varied favourite foods that do not burn the mouth (egg, mashed potato, pumpkin, avocado), small frequent feeds when the child is alert, and active feeding on the mother's lap.

read.title: Stopping breastfeeding: gradually, over one month

steps.title: Plan ahead
steps.text: Discuss why she wants to stop, and what food and milk she will give instead. Crying does not mean she has too little milk.

steps.title: Prepare the baby
steps.text: Teach the baby to drink expressed breast milk from a cup (boiled if mother and baby are not on ARVs). Replace one breastfeed with one cup feed, then more every few days. A clean finger can replace the breast for sucking.

steps.title: Stop completely
steps.text: Stop as soon as the baby is used to frequent cup feeds. Do not start again: it raises the risk of HIV. Express a little milk and use cold compresses when the breasts feel full.

steps.title: Continue ARV prophylaxis
steps.text: Continue it for one week after the baby has had no breast milk at all, and make sure she has enough.

steps.title: Family planning and CD4
steps.text: Start family planning before breastfeeding ends. Check she has had a CD4 count in the past 6 months.

cards.back: Help her make a safe and complete change to replacement feeds; arrange formula (under 6 months) or plain milk if she has no resources. Refer her for ART and give cotrimoxazole.
A suitable breast milk substitute, breast milk from a confirmed HIV-negative woman, or pasteurized milk from a breast milk bank.
Safe family foods and milk or another animal-source food every day.

read.text: A mother stopped breastfeeding completely 3 days ago. How long does the baby's ARV prophylaxis continue?
options: Until one week after the last breast milk

sections.title: Counsel the mother on her own health

read.text: Counsel an HIV-infected mother on her own health, and counsel Lungile.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text: During a sick child visit, listen for the mother's own problems, and write them at the bottom of the recording form so you remember to help her after the child. Do not make her queue twice or go elsewhere for simple problems.

cards.back: Care for her, or refer her for ART.
Engorgement, sore nipples or infection: give care or refer.
Eat well to keep up her own strength and health.
Check her immunization and give TT if needed.
Discuss methods, offer barrier contraception as well, and give at least 3 months' supply.
Screen and treat by the national STI protocol; counsel on safe sex.
Regular CD4 testing (every 6 months), sexual health services and counselling.
Partner, family, housing, childcare, workload: give ongoing counselling, refer if needed.

read.text: If she is HIV-infected, reassure her that with regular follow-up much can be done to keep her and her child well; stress good hygiene and early treatment of illness.

stages.text: Peter is 6 months old, breastfeeding, and not low weight for age.
stages.question: What feeding advice do you give Lungile?
options: Breastfeed as often as he wants, and give 3 servings of complementary food a day plus 1 snack
Stop breastfeeding now and give formula
stages.explanation: At 6 up to 12 months: breastfeed on demand, with 3 adequate servings of nutritious complementary foods a day plus one snack, 3/4 cup each. She has eggs, potatoes, squash and some chicken: you show her how to make porridge and feed Peter with a spoon, and ask checking questions.

stages.text: Lungile has just found out she has HIV. She lives alone in a tin shack in the city, fetching water from a tap 200 metres away. Her partner works in another city. Neither he nor her mother knows her status; she is scared to tell her partner.
stages.question: What do you discuss today?
options: The most important topics, and encourage her to continue counselling and HIV care
Everything about HIV in one session
Nothing: it is not your role
stages.explanation: Her health, access to care, feeding and breast problems, immunization, nutrition, STIs, family planning and hygiene. Her other clinic already covers some of these, so you discuss them briefly. She worries she has too little milk, so you discuss that.

read.text: Practise
Explain what ART does, why three drugs are used, and name the common ARV drugs.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text: HIV is a retrovirus, so the drugs against it are antiretroviral drugs (ARVs). They interfere with the life cycle of the virus so it cannot make copies of itself. Giving ARVs correctly, with adherence support, is antiretroviral therapy (ART).
ART does NOT cure HIV. By stopping the virus from multiplying, it prevents damage to the immune system and improves quality of life and life expectancy.
read.label: Key point

read.text: Children's bodies handle ARVs differently, so doses are adjusted to weight as the child grows.

cards.front: It takes a lot of force
cards.back: HIV makes new copies very fast. One drug slows it; three together have a very powerful effect.
ARVs from different groups attack the virus at different steps of making copies.
HIV can change so a drug works less well. With three drugs together, it takes much longer for resistance to develop.

read.text:
GroupExamples
Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NsRTI)lamivudine (3TC), stavudine (d4T), zidovudine (AZT), didanosine (ddI), abacavir (ABC)
Nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NtRTI)tenofovir (TDF)
Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTI)nevirapine (NVP), efavirenz (EFV)
Protease inhibitors (PI)lopinavir (LPV), indinavir, atazanavir, darunavir; ritonavir (RTV) boosts another PI
First-line regimens usually include 2 NsRTIs and 1 NNRTI or a boosted PI. Stavudine was used as a first-line drug and many children still take it, but it is no longer preferred.
Stavudine is no longer used. Since 2019 to 2021 WHO prefers dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens for most children. Use the current national ART guidelines.
read.label: Changed since 2014

read.text: Which statement about ART is correct?
options: ART stops HIV multiplying but does not cure it

sections.title: Starting ART: confirm infection and check the caregiver

read.text: Follow the first three of the five steps for starting ART, and decide which children are eligible.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text: A child with a general danger sign or a severe classification needs URGENT REFERRAL. ART is not urgent: start it once the child is stable (acute illnesses and opportunistic infections treated) and the five steps are completed.

read.title: The five steps of starting ART

steps.title: Step 1: confirm HIV infection
steps.text: Under 18 months: a positive virological (PCR) test, and the child has not breastfed for at least 6 weeks. 18 months or older: two different positive serological tests. If results disagree, refer.

steps.title: Step 2: the caregiver is able to give ART
steps.text: She is willing and able, and ideally has disclosed to another adult who can help, or is in a support group. If not: classify CONFIRMED HIV INFECTION not on ART, follow up and support her until she is ready.

steps.title: Step 3: can ART start at your facility?
steps.text: If the child weighs less than 3 kg or has TB, refer non-urgently for ART. Otherwise go to step 4.

steps.title: Step 4: record baseline information
steps.text: Weight, height and nutrition, pallor, feeding, clinical stage, and laboratory results. Do not wait for results.

steps.title: Step 5: start ART and cotrimoxazole
steps.text: With routine treatments, and follow up after one week.

read.text: All children under 5 years with CONFIRMED HIV INFECTION are eligible for ART. From 5 years, WHO 2014 used a CD4 count below 500 (priority below 350) or clinical stage 3 or 4.
read.label: Key point

read.text: WHO now recommends ART for every child living with HIV, at any age and any CD4 count.
read.label: Changed since 2014

read.title: Who starts ART at a first-level facility?

cards.back: A stable child: not ill, and no signs of advanced HIV infection.
A child under 3 kg (doses are hard), or a child with TB or suspected TB (needs investigations and dose changes). Non-urgent means soon, but not necessarily the same day.

read.text: Practise

sections.title: Prepare the caregiver for adherence: the 5 As

read.text: Use the 5 As to prepare a caregiver to give ART every day.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text: Adherence is the cornerstone of ART: at least 95% of doses must be taken.
read.label: Key point

read.text: Why is adherence harder for children?
read.answer: Children depend on their caregivers; parents may not want to disclose the status; there are few easy child formulations, so mixtures of pills and syrups are needed; and many medicines taste bad.

read.text: These social criteria are not a barrier to ART, but part of preparing for it: at least one caregiver who can supervise the medicine, and, if possible, disclosure to another adult in the same house who can help.

steps.title: 1. ASSESS
steps.text: Find a treatment supporter. Check the caregiver understands that ART is lifelong and has side effects.

steps.title: 2. ADVISE
steps.text: Be open, non-judgmental and patient: "I have some information about HIV and ART. Would you like to hear it?" Explain how the illness progresses and that the child's life depends on the correct dose twice a day at the right time. Do not give too much at once: spread the advice over several visits.

steps.title: 3. AGREE
steps.text: Check she is willing and motivated: "After hearing all this, how do you think your child will be able to take this treatment?" Has she kept appointments and given other medicines? Does she take her own treatment?

steps.title: 4. ASSIST
steps.text: "What problems might arise?" Help with transport and time off work, giving medicine without stigma, family support, disclosure and an adherence support group.

steps.title: 5. ARRANGE
steps.text: Arrange another session to reinforce key messages, and a support group if she wishes.

read.text: Preparing a caregiver usually takes 2 to 3 visits, the clinical team and a treatment supporter.
read.label: Remember

read.text: Which of the 5 As is this?

items.text: Ask if there is someone who can help give the medicine
Explain that the medicine must be given twice a day at the same time
Ask how she thinks her child will manage the treatment
Plan how she will get to the clinic each month
Book the next counselling session

cards.back: Assess and classify. A severe classification needs referral; manage others by the charts. Do not delay ART.
Assess feeding of all children under 2, children with acute malnutrition, and all young infants.
Stage the child from 1 to 4 (see the staging lesson).
At diagnosis, before ART if possible, and every 6 months on ART. Send it if not done in the last 3 months. Viral load is useful but not essential.

read.text: Practise
Name the common and the serious side effects of each ARV, and say what to do about each one.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text: Most side effects are mild, especially at the start; fewer than 5% of patients have serious ones. Caregivers who know about side effects are less likely to stop the medicine.

DrugVery common (advise how to manage)Potentially serious (seek care)Later in treatment
Stavudine (d4T)Nausea, diarrhoeaUrgently: severe abdominal pain and difficulty breathing. Soon: tingling, numb or painful feet, legs or handsChanges in fat distribution
Abacavir (ABC)Urgently: fever, vomiting and rash (hypersensitivity)
Lamivudine (3TC)Nausea, diarrhoea
Lopinavir/ritonavirNausea, vomiting, diarrhoeaRaised cholesterol and glucose; changes in fat distribution
Nevirapine (NVP)Nausea, diarrhoeaUrgently: yellow eyes, severe skin rash, fatigue and shortness of breath, fever
Zidovudine (AZT)Nausea, diarrhoea, headache, fatigue, muscle painUrgently: pallor (anaemia)
Efavirenz (EFV)Nausea, diarrhoea, strange dreams, poor sleep, memory problems, headache, dizzinessUrgently: yellow eyes, psychosis or confusion, severe skin rash
Never stop just one or two drugs, or give a lower dose. If a side effect is so bad that the mother wants to stop, she comes to the clinic; if no clinician is available, STOP ALL THREE drugs.
read.label: Key point

cards.back: Stop the drugs and REFER URGENTLY.
On abacavir, assess carefully and call for advice. Severe, generalized or peeling rash, rash on the mucosa, or rash with fever or vomiting: stop the drugs and REFER URGENTLY.
Give the drug with food. If it lasts more than 2 weeks or worsens, call for advice or refer.
Repeat the dose if the medicine is seen in the vomit or vomiting was within 30 minutes. Vomiting everything, or with severe abdominal pain or difficult breathing: REFER URGENTLY.
Use the diarrhoea charts. If due to ARVs it improves in a few weeks; if not after 2 weeks, call for advice or refer.
Paracetamol for headache. Give efavirenz at night on an empty stomach or with low-fat food. If it lasts more than 2 weeks, call for advice or refer.
If new or worse on treatment, call for advice or refer.
Consider switching from stavudine to abacavir; refer if needed.

steps.title: Introduce
steps.text: Discuss common side effects before the child starts.

steps.title: Advise
steps.text: Explain how to manage them.

steps.title: Warn
steps.text: Name the serious ones that need urgent care.

steps.title: Respond
steps.text: Give immediate attention, at the clinic or by phone.

steps.title: Ask
steps.text: Ask about side effects at every follow-up, even if not mentioned.

steps.title: Support
steps.text: Refer to peer educators.

read.text: Practise
Follow Peter's care from HIV EXPOSED to confirmed infection, and start him on ART.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

stages.text: Each month Peter gets routine care (vitamin A, immunizations, growth monitoring, feeding counselling), continues cotrimoxazole, has new problems treated, and you ask about Lungile's health.
Lungile stops breastfeeding when Peter is 9 months old, because she now works away from home. They return 7 weeks after his last breastfeed.
stages.question: Which test now confirms Peter's status?
stages.explanation: Peter is under 18 months and has not breastfed for more than 6 weeks: a virological test confirms his status.

stages.text: You counsel Lungile, discuss disclosure and send a PCR test. Two and a half weeks later the result is positive. Lungile feels guilty that she made Peter sick; you counsel her that treatment can keep him healthy.
stages.question: How do you classify Peter now?
stages.explanation: A positive virological test, more than 6 weeks after the last breastfeed: CONFIRMED HIV INFECTION. All children under 5 with confirmed infection should receive ART.

stages.text: Peter is stable: he needs no treatment today for an acute illness or opportunistic infection. Step 1: his infection is confirmed.

Step 2: you use the 5 As with Lungile: her social situation and understanding of HIV, key information about ART and adherence, whether she can give the medicine every day and come to appointments, her support, and another session.
Step 3: Peter has no TB and weighs more than 3 kg.
stages.question: Where does Peter start ART?

stages.text: Step 4: Peter is not low weight and not anaemic. He has had pneumonia, persistent diarrhoea and ear infections in the past months, and herpes zoster is starting. You send CD4 and viral load tests.
Step 5: Peter is under 3 years and weighs 7.2 kg.
stages.question: Which regimen and doses?
options: ABC 4 ml + 3TC 4 ml + LPV/r 1.5 ml, each twice a day
ABC 6 ml + 3TC 6 ml + LPV/r 2 ml, each twice a day
stages.explanation: Under 3 years: ABC + 3TC + LPV/r. The 6 to 9.9 kg band is 4 ml, 4 ml and 1.5 ml twice a day. He also continues cotrimoxazole. You tell Lungile about side effects, and see him after one week.

read.text: Practise

sections.title: Follow-up of exposed infants and good chronic care

read.text: Make sure exposed infants are tested and followed up, and use the principles of good chronic care.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text: Every child born to an HIV-infected mother needs follow-up for safe feeding, growth and development, HIV testing and other care. Offer a PCR test at 4 to 6 weeks (for example at the immunization visit), start cotrimoxazole, and ask the caregiver to return for the result. Reclassify the child when the result is known, and give care for the new classification.
How can a clinic find more HIV-exposed infants?
read.answer: Have a system in every clinic to identify infants and offer testing. Integrated maternal and child health clinics see mothers and children together; a family-based model links the records of the whole family, so when a parent comes you ask about the children and partner.

read.text: HIV is a chronic disease. Good chronic care recognizes that the mother must learn to manage her child's condition, often while coping with her own illness: a double burden.

1. Develop a treatment partnership with the mother and child
  2. Focus on their concerns and priorities
  3. Use IMCI counselling skills and the 5 As
  4. Support self-management
  5. Organize proactive follow-up
  6. Involve expert patients, peer educators and support staff
  7. Link the family to community resources and support
  8. Use written information to document, monitor and remind
  9. Work as a multidisciplinary clinical team
  10. Assure continuity of care

cards.back: An agreement to work together towards an agreed goal: both share responsibility and treat each other with respect; one partner does not have all the power.
Find out the real reason she came: illness, fear, or a psychosocial need, and address it.
Leave the mother as much in charge as possible: she takes responsibility for daily treatment, and feels more in control.
A nurse, clinical officer, an ART aid for education and adherence, and a doctor.

read.text: Practise

sections.title: Follow-up of a child on ART: the four steps

read.text: Follow up a child on ART in four steps, and know when to refer urgently or non-urgently.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.title: Follow-up of a child on ART
read.caption: Watch this first.

read.title: The four steps of each follow-up visit

steps.title: 1. Assess and classify
steps.text: Ask about problems and care elsewhere since the last visit. Check general danger signs, ART severe signs and the main symptoms.

steps.title: 2. Monitor progress on ART and cotrimoxazole
steps.text: Growth and nutrition, development, adherence, side effects, clinical stage and laboratory results.

steps.title: 3. Continue ART and other medicines
steps.text: If stable, continue the same first-line regimen, adjusting doses to weight.

steps.title: 4. Counsel
steps.text: Progress, feeding, adherence, side effects, disclosure, support for the caregiver; check the family gets care. If well, follow up in one month.

read.text: ART severe signs: severe skin rash; difficulty breathing with severe abdominal pain; yellow eyes; or two of fever, vomiting and rash in a child on abacavir. Give pre-referral treatment and REFER URGENTLY.
read.label: Key point

read.text: How often does the child miss doses?

items.text: No dose missed this month
One dose missed last week
Two doses missed each week
Three or more doses missed each week

read.explanation: Poor adherence means missing more than two doses a week. Ask kindly when the last dose was missed; a pill count can help. Praise good adherence at every visit.

read.text:
Viral load (copies/ml)Meaning and action
Below 400ART is working well. Routine follow-up; repeat after a year.
400 to 1000Improvement needed. Step up adherence counselling; repeat after 6 months.
Above 1000ARVs not working well (poor adherence or resistance). Step up counselling, repeat after 3 months; if still above 1000, refer.

CD4 count and percentage are repeated after 6 months, after 1 year, then every year. Normal CD4 counts are higher in young children, so they cannot be read like an adult's. Lack of laboratory tests should never stop a child from receiving ART.

cards.back: Not gaining weight for 3 months, or losing milestones.
Poor adherence despite counselling.
Significant side effects despite good management.
A higher clinical stage than before, CD4 much lower than before, or viral load above 400 despite counselling (on LPV/r: LDL above 3.5 or triglycerides above 5.6 mmol/L).

read.text: A new or recurrent stage 3 or 4 event after at least 24 weeks of ART, in a child who takes the medicine well, may mean treatment failure. Only experienced clinicians change to second-line treatment.
Replace stavudine when fat changes appear, support disclosure to the child, and follow up children on ART.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text: Nurses at primary level prescribe only first-line regimens and do not change ARVs without an expert, with one exception: stavudine. It causes peripheral neuropathy (tingling in the hands and feet) and lipodystrophy: the arms, legs, buttocks and cheeks become THIN while the breasts, tummy and back of the neck become FAT. This may not go away, so switch early to abacavir. A child doing well on stavudine stays on it.
Disclosure to the child

Disclosing the HIV status to the child is the caregiver's role, with support from the health worker. It is a process, not an event: partial disclosure first (without naming HIV, for example the "soldier story"), then full disclosure over time, fitted to the child's understanding, development, health and situation. There is no fixed age; questions about the clinic or the medicine, or refusing treatment, are signs the child wants to know more. Adolescents should know their status.

cards.back: Better adjustment, self-esteem and adherence, fewer risky behaviours, and stronger family ties.
Less part in treatment, more psychological problems, isolation, hurtful fantasies about the illness, and accidental disclosure that breaks the child's trust in adults.

stages.text: There are no new problems and no care elsewhere. Peter has no general danger sign, no main symptom, and no severe skin rash, difficult breathing, yellow eyes, fever or vomiting. You screen for TB.

He has gained a little weight, to 7.4 kg. Lungile has given every dose and brought the containers. There is no change in side effects or stage. His CD4 count is 600 cells/mm3, and the viral load is detectable but not high.
stages.question: What do you do?
options: Continue the same ART and cotrimoxazole, praise her, counsel and arrange the next visit
stages.explanation: Peter is stable. Counsel on his progress, adherence (his viral load is still detectable), side effects, disclosure and support.

read.text: Practise
Stage a child with confirmed HIV infection using the WHO paediatric clinical staging.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text: Clinical staging estimates how damaged a child's immune system is, from the child's signs and symptoms (and laboratory tests if possible). Use it only for children with confirmed HIV infection. Choose the highest stage that applies. Stages 1 and 2: the immune system is not yet seriously affected and most conditions are managed at first level. Stages 3 and 4: advanced immune deficiency; most conditions need urgent referral.

read.title: The four stages (WHO 2005 revised paediatric staging)

cards.back: No symptoms, or only persistent generalized lymphadenopathy.

Enlarged liver or spleen, enlarged parotid, skin conditions (prurigo, seborrhoeic dermatitis, extensive molluscum or warts, fungal nail infection, herpes zoster), recurrent mouth ulcers, angular cheilitis, gum erythema, recurrent or chronic respiratory infections (sinusitis, ear infections, otorrhoea).

Moderate unexplained malnutrition not responding to treatment; oral thrush (after the newborn period); oral hairy leukoplakia; unexplained diarrhoea over 14 days or fever over 1 month not responding to treatment; recurrent severe bacterial pneumonia; pulmonary or lymph node TB; symptomatic LIP; necrotizing gingivitis; chronic HIV lung disease; anaemia, neutropenia or low platelets for over a month.

Severe unexplained wasting, stunting or malnutrition not responding to treatment; PCP; oesophageal thrush; herpes simplex ulcers for over a month; 2 or more severe bacterial infections a year (not pneumonia); Kaposi's sarcoma; extrapulmonary TB; toxoplasma brain abscess; cryptococcal meningitis; HIV encephalopathy; rectal fistula.

read.text: Children are staged even when they are on ART, because a change of stage shows how they respond. A child with suspected severe HIV disease whose infection cannot be confirmed needs referral.
read.label: Remember

read.text: Which stage is this condition?

items.text: Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy only
Herpes zoster
Recurrent ear discharge
Oral thrush in a 2-year-old
Pulmonary TB
Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP)
Oesophageal thrush

read.text: Practise
Answer the review questions, then the logbook test.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content

read.text:
Look back at the main points:

  • A positive serological test cannot confirm HIV under 18 months; a positive virological test confirms it at any age.
  • A negative test only rules out infection once the child has not breastfed for at least 6 weeks.
  • Three classifications: CONFIRMED HIV INFECTION, HIV EXPOSED, HIV INFECTION UNLIKELY.
  • Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis for exposed and infected children; ARV prophylaxis for exposed infants; IPT, immunization and vitamin A.
  • All children under 5 with confirmed infection start ART after the five steps; adherence of at least 95% is essential.
  • Each follow-up visit of a child on ART has four steps; ART severe signs need urgent referral.
Answer the same questions as before the module.
Then take the logbook test. You may use your chart booklet, but not the module.
Look back on what you learned, plan how you will use it, and tell us what you think. When you finish this lesson the module badge is yours.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: This lesson follows the WHO 2014 module and chart booklet for high HIV settings. The Sudan national IMNCI booklet has no HIV section, so this is not Sudan national guidance. HIV testing, prophylaxis and ART recommendations have changed since 2014: in practice, follow the current Sudan national HIV guidelines.
read.label: WHO 2014 HIV content
Recap
read.text:
What you learned

  • Know the HIV status of the child and the mother.
  • Give cotrimoxazole prophylaxis and the right feeding advice to HIV-exposed children.
  • Support adherence to ART and follow up regularly.

In your clinic this week, record in your logbook three children you see for HIV exposure or infection: what you found, how you classified them and what you did. Bring the logbook to your next supervision visit or course session.
read.label: Your logbook

prompts: What is one thing you will do differently in your clinic after this module?
Which part was hardest for you? What will you practise again?
read.ratingText: How useful was this module for your work?

modules.title: Module 9: Care of the well child

read.text: See what well child care covers, and take the pre-test.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: A well child is a child who comes to the health facility for preventive services: immunizations, feeding advice, and growth and development monitoring. You use the same IMNCI skills as for the sick child: ask questions, listen, praise good practices, advise in simple language, and check understanding. Even when the clinic is busy, take time to assess a well child properly.

More than 200 million children under 5 are not developing to their full potential because they did not get simple, essential care. Risks include stunting, iron and iodine deficiency, frequent illness, and too little help to learn, explore and communicate.
What you will practise

• Feeding infants and young children well
  • Care for healthy growth and development
  • Immunization, vitamin A and deworming
  • Water, sanitation and hygiene
  • Prevention of childhood accidents
Which part of the recording form is used in this module?

read.caption: The national recording form: immunization and feeding

read.text: Before you begin

sections.title: Growth and development: what they are

read.text: Tell growth from development, and name the four kinds of skills a child develops.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Care of the well child
read.caption: Watch this first.

cards.back: An increase in physical size, composition and distribution of tissues: weight, length and height.

The gradual unfolding of what a child can do: talk, walk, run, solve problems, receive affection and express emotions. It needs good health and nutrition, chances to explore, and a safe, nurturing home.
Physical skills such as reaching and grabbing: planned eye and hand movement, muscle control and strength.
Exploring and learning through seeing, hearing, moving and touching; recognizing people, things and sounds; comparing sizes and shapes.
Communicating interests and needs, with words and without.
Receiving and expressing emotions and affection appropriately.

read.text: Which skill is the child using?

items.text: Sees a ball rolling and tries to take and hold it
Cries and reaches for the ball when it rolls away
Examines the ball's shape and size
Smiles at his mother when she talks to him about the ball

read.text: Health workers need to understand growth and development to monitor progress, find delays early, counsel caregivers and treat. Poor growth and development can also reflect poverty, little education, and poor access to food, safe water and health services.

sections.title: Growth monitoring: why, what and how often

read.text: Explain growth monitoring and promotion, name the three growth indicators, and know how often to measure.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Growth monitoring and promotion (GMP) detects poor growth early, so it can be corrected. It is not only measuring: you use the results to counsel the caregiver on what she can do at home.

GMP helps you to:

  • Analyse the causes of poor growth: acute or chronic illness, acute malnutrition, feeding problems
  • Show the caregiver the child's growth on the growth chart
  • Agree with the caregiver on actions at home, early
  • Link families to community and nutrition services
  • Keep the child in regular contact with the clinic

cards.back: Low = UNDERWEIGHT. Changes quickly with health, so it is the measure used to monitor growth in infants and young children.
Low = STUNTING (chronic malnutrition): the result of long-term poor nutrition.
Low = WASTING (acute malnutrition), as in Module 6.

read.text:
AgeHow often
Birth to 2 yearsMonthly: weight every month, length every 3 months
2 to 5 yearsEvery 3 months: weight and height at every visit

cards.back: Length (lying) under 2 years; height (standing) from 2 years. Under 2 measured standing: add 0.7 cm. 2 years or older measured lying: subtract 0.7 cm.
A solar, taring scale (it can subtract the mother's weight). A Salter scale can be used until one is available.
A wooden length board in two or three pieces, joined for a tall child.
Growth charts for each visit, and the schedules for vaccines, vitamin A and deworming. Separate books for boys and girls.

read.text: Use every growth monitoring visit, in the clinic or at outreach, to give other services: assessment, treatment, vaccination, vitamin A, deworming and psychosocial support.
Use the child health book with the caregiver, and decide whether a child's growth and development are normal.
read.label: In this lesson

steps.title: Why
steps.text: Explain why growth matters, even if the child looks healthy next to the other children at home.

steps.title: The book
steps.text: Explain the child health book. Every child should get one soon after birth; bring it to every visit.

steps.title: The chart
steps.text: Use the growth chart to show how the child is growing, and the pattern over time.

steps.title: What else is due
steps.text: Show the feeding advice and the schedules in the book, and remind her of the services due today.

read.text: The mother's health is important for the child's health. Ask about her pregnancy, delivery and health since.
read.label: Remember

stages.text: Samson comes for growth monitoring and vitamin A. He weighs 8 kg and is 64 cm long. On the boys' chart, 8 kg at 64 cm is above the median line.
stages.question: What do you tell his mother?
options: He is growing well; praise her and continue

stages.text: Jandika comes for growth monitoring. He weighs 8 kg and is 71 cm long. His weight-for-length is between 0 and -1: not wasted. But on the length-for-age chart he is below -3.
stages.question: What does this show, and what do you do?
options: Severe stunting: refer (not urgently) to find and treat the cause
stages.explanation: Advise his mother not to delay the hospital visit.

read.text: Explain bonding and attachment to a caregiver, and tell sensitivity from responsiveness.
read.label: In this lesson

cards.back: The mother forms a relationship with her new baby, starting in the first hours after birth. Harmed by long separation after birth, poor health or depression of the mother (often undetected), abuse or neglect, or a low birth weight or sick baby.
The baby forms a relationship with the mother or main caregiver during the first two years, especially at 2 to 7 months, and develops a personal way of communicating with her.

read.text:
Poor attachment can lead to:

  • Difficulty trusting others; depression or rage
  • Failure to thrive, physically and emotionally
  • Difficulty adapting to change
  • Later, behaviour problems, poor relations with peers, poor problem solving and low self-esteem

cards.back: Being aware of the baby's signals and reading them correctly; accepting the child's interests; seeing the child as a separate person, from his point of view.
Responding to the signal quickly and appropriately, for example seeing that the baby is hungry and feeding him. A caregiver must be sensitive to be responsive.

read.text: Sara and her son John: sensitivity or responsiveness?

items.text: Sara hears John crying
Sara picks John up to soothe his crying
While bathing John, Sara notices a rash on his leg
Sara sees John watching the branches blowing in the wind
Sara says: "Do you see the wind blowing? The leaves are blowing!"
Sara notices John is feeding less than usual
Sara offers John a food he likes to see if he will eat

read.text: Sara's grandmother says John should be left alone so he grows strong and independent. What do you tell Sara?
read.answer: Explain the benefits of bonding and attachment for John's growth and for his skills, with clear examples Sara can share with her grandmother: a child who is answered when he signals grows more secure, curious and able to learn.

read.text: Recommend play and communication activities for the child's age, and show how to make toys at home.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Play and communication activities stimulate learning, improve care (including feeding), strengthen the caregiver's skills, and improve the interaction between caregiver and child.

read.title: Care for child development
read.caption: WHO Care for Child Development CD: case stories on child development.

cards.back: Play: let the baby see, hear, feel, move arms and legs freely and touch you; skin-to-skin; gently soothe and stroke. Communicate: look into the baby's eyes and talk, also during breastfeeding.
Play: move colourful things for the baby to see and reach; a shaker rattle, a ring on a string. Communicate: smile and laugh, talk, copy the baby's sounds and gestures.
Play: clean, safe household things to handle, bang and drop: containers with lids, a metal pot and spoon. Communicate: respond to sounds and interests; call the child's name and see the response.
Play: hide a toy and let the child find it; peek-a-boo; a doll with a face. Communicate: name things and people; teach gestures like waving bye-bye.
Play: things to stack and to put in and out of containers. Communicate: ask simple questions; respond to attempts to talk; show and talk about nature, pictures and people.
Play: pictures, face puzzles, shapes to sort by colour, a soft ball, chalk and a flat stone, a home-made book. Communicate: encourage the child to talk and tell stories; answer questions.

read.text: Toys do not need to be bought. Make some at the clinic from jars, stones, cloth, cardboard and old magazines, and show caregivers how easy they are to make and use.

read.title: Using the chart with a caregiver

steps.title: Find the age
steps.text: Find the child's age group and its activities, and explain the chart.

steps.title: Teach
steps.text: Explain how to play and communicate, demonstrate, then watch her practise and give feedback.

steps.title: At home
steps.text: Explain how to use the activities regularly at home, and ask checking questions.

read.text: Which is a good checking question?
options: What activities can you do to play with your child?
Did the nurse explain how to play with your child?
read.explanation: It cannot be answered yes or no.

read.text: Beta says her son Rakim, 4 months, is too little to understand play or talk. What do you say?
read.answer: Development begins at birth: even in his first hours a baby connects with people and his surroundings. Show Beta how Rakim already communicates and plays now: following her voice, reaching, smiling.

read.text: Use the milestone chart to find a child whose development is delayed.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Each stage of development has milestones: skills a child should have at that age. Use them to monitor development, and teach caregivers the simple milestones so delays are found early. A child with delayed milestones is referred for further management.

AgeGross motorFine motorSpeech and languageAdaptive and social

2 monthsProne, arms extended forwardPulls at clothesCoos
4 monthsRaises head and chest, rolls front to back, no head lagReaches and grasps, objects to mouthResponds to voice

9 monthsPulls to standFinger-thumb graspMama, dada, imitates one wordPlays games, separation anxiety

read.title: How to check some milestones in the clinic

cards.back: Lay the child face up and gently pull to sitting by both hands; make a sound with keys; ask the mother to make a joyful sound. The child holds the head up, turns it, responds to voice and smiles.
Sit the child on a safe flat surface with a toy to hold. The child sits without using the hands for at least 10 seconds, and brings objects to the mouth.
Stand the child holding a support at abdomen height: the legs carry the weight for 10 seconds. The child crawls towards a toy, imitates bye-bye, passes objects hand to hand.
The child walks at least 5 steps alone, climbs stairs with help, throws a ball, says 4–20 words, drinks from a cup.
Short phrases, kicks a ball on request, jumps with both feet, turns pages one at a time, points to named pictures.

stages.text: Manka was born at term 5 months ago. She got neck control at 5 months and cannot yet sit without support. Her mother is worried.
stages.question: What do you advise?
options: This can be normal: children sit without support at 5 to 7 months; keep coming for monitoring

stages.text: Ikupa is 36 months old. She walks only with support, says about 10 words and drinks from a cup.
stages.question: What do you advise?
options: Her milestones are those of 8 to 11 months: refer (not urgently) for assessment within a few days
stages.explanation: At 3 years she should run, jump, stand on one foot and use plurals.

read.text: Build the mother's confidence, then counsel on common feeding problems and follow them up.
read.label: In this lesson

steps.title: Build confidence first
steps.text: Praise good feeding practices; encourage her to feed the same way in illness and health. Avoid judgemental words.

steps.title: Counsel for the age
steps.text: If the child is entering a new age group, explain the new recommendations (for example, at almost 6 months, good complementary foods and when to start).

steps.title: Explain what is not followed
steps.text: Explain the recommendations that are not being followed, and make suggestions.

cards.back: Check and improve positioning and attachment (Module 2). A breast problem may need a trained breastfeeding counsellor.

cards.front: Under 6 months, other milk or foods
cards.back: Aim to return to more or exclusive breastfeeding: more frequent, longer breastfeeds day and night, and gradually reduce other milk or food. If breastfeeding is not possible, teach correct preparation of breast-milk substitutes, used within one hour.
Recommend a cup: it is easier to keep clean and does not interfere with breastfeeding.
Sit with the child and encourage him to eat. He needs his own serving, not a shared plate with siblings.
Offer the foods recommended for his age, as often as recommended; breastfeed more often and longer; small, frequent, soft, liked foods. Discourage snacks and juices that only fill him up.

read.text:
Encourage a young child to eat

  • Offer small amounts when the child is alert and happy, and more if he shows interest
  • Food of suitable consistency, not too thick or dry
  • A suitable spoon, food within reach, the child on the caregiver's lap
  • Encourage with words, smiles and songs. A child who gets more attention for refusing food may eat less.

Sudan national booklet: Follow up a FEEDING PROBLEM in 7 days: reassess feeding, ask how she has carried out the advice, and counsel on any new or continuing problem. WHO module (page 39): Follow-up in 5 days; if the child is very low weight for age, also return 30 days after the first visit to check weight gain.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

stages.text: At the first visit, a 3-month-old was getting 2 or 3 bottles of milk a day and some breastfeeds. The health worker advised more frequent, longer breastfeeds and less other milk. Now the mother gives 1 bottle a day and breastfeeds 6 or more times in 24 hours.
stages.question: What do you do?
options: Praise her, then suggest stopping the other milk and breastfeeding 8 or more times in 24 hours, and see her again

read.text: Give the feeding recommendations for the child's age, in sickness and in health.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: First ask how the child is fed now; then give only the advice needed for the child's age and situation. The recommendations are the same when the child is sick and when well. During illness offer the recommended foods as often as recommended; after illness, good feeding makes up the weight lost.
Use the national mother card for your counselling. The age groups below are those of the WHO module.

cards.back: Breastfeed exclusively, as often as the child wants, day and night, at least 8 times in 24 hours. No other food or fluid, not even water (medicines and vitamins only if needed).

Breastfeed as often as the child wants, breast milk first. Start 2–3 teaspoons of soft porridge or mashed food and build up: 3 meals plus healthy snacks a day if breastfed, 5 meals if not. Not breastfed: formula, or 3 cups of full-cream cow's milk from 9 months.

Breastfeed as often as the child wants. Complementary or chopped and mashed family foods 5 times a day, with protein at least once a day and fruit or vegetables twice. Not breastfed: full-cream milk every day. Active feeding.
Family foods, 3 meals a day plus 2 nutritious snacks between meals (bread with peanut butter, fruit, full-cream milk). Continue active feeding; offer a refused food several times.

read.text:
Include all food groups

  • Cereals, roots and tubers: rice, wheat, maize, millet, sorghum, cassava, potatoes
  • Animal foods and legumes: meat, chicken, fish, eggs, milk, cheese, yoghurt, chickpeas, lentils, beans
  • Green leafy and orange vegetables; fruits, mashed
  • Oils and fats, preferably seed oils such as groundnut or sunflower

NutrientFoods
IronGreen leafy vegetables, fish, meat, chicken, liver or kidney, eggs
ZincFish, meat, chicken, liver or kidney, eggs
Vitamin ADark-coloured fruits and vegetables, red palm oil
Vitamin CMany fruits and vegetables, potatoes
FolateLegumes, green leafy vegetables, orange juice

cards.back: Clean hands, utensils, water and food; boil drinking water and milk; keep food well cooked and covered.
Ready-made jars of baby food (costly, unreliable, often lacking nutrients), fruit juice, tea and sugary drinks.
Feed slowly and patiently, without forcing; own serving; eye contact and talk. An adequate serving means the child wants no more after active feeding.

read.text: Apply the feeding recommendations to real situations.
read.label: In this lesson

stages.text: Her mother returned to work a month ago, is away 10 hours a day, and stopped breastfeeding. The child takes infant formula by cup about 5 times a day and plain cereal 3 times a day, and has eaten as usual during this illness.
stages.question: Which comment praises what she does right?
options: It is good that you use a cup instead of a bottle
You should still be breastfeeding this child

stages.question: Which advice improves her diet?
options: The cereal is good: add a little oil and mashed vegetables, peas or bits of meat

read.text: Greg, 10 months, is breastfed. He has porridge once a day and jars of baby fruit and vegetables twice. What do you suggest?
options: 4–5 servings of nutritious food a day; add oil, margarine or groundnut paste to the porridge; spend the jar money on eggs, fruit and vegetables
Keep the jars: they are complete

read.text: Fatima, 14 months, has PNEUMONIA and ANAEMIA and often gets chest infections. Which nutrients matter most?
read.explanation: Iron: liver, meat, fish, legumes, dark green leaves. Vitamin A: liver, mango, pawpaw, sweet potato, dark green leaves.

read.text: Joyce, 3 months, is exclusively breastfed, and also gets water. What do you say?
options: She needs no water: breast milk gives all the fluid she needs
Water is good in hot weather

read.text: Xoli, 15 months, breastfeeds and eats rice, meat, vegetables, fruit and yoghurt. How often should he eat these foods?
Counsel a family on safe water, hand washing and a clean, safe place to play.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: About 9 out of 10 cases of diarrhoea come from unsafe water or poor sanitation and hygiene, which also lead to pneumonia and worms that cause anaemia. The key interventions are cheap: safe drinking water, hand washing, and toilets in the home and community.

cards.back: Before preparing food, before eating, before feeding a child.
After using the toilet, and after cleaning a child who has used it.
After coughing, sneezing or blowing the nose; before and after cleaning a child's face; after handling animals, animal waste or rubbish.

read.text:
How

  • Use soap. Rub hands together, between the fingers and under the nails, for 20 seconds (sing "Happy Birthday" twice).
  • Pour water over the hands: do not dip them into a bowl, which contaminates the water.

steps.title: Ask
steps.text: Where do you wash your hands? Is there soap? When do you wash them?

steps.title: Plan
steps.text: Help them prepare a convenient place with water and soap.

steps.title: Teach
steps.text: Review when to wash, demonstrate, and let the caregiver practise.

read.text: Babies explore by putting things in the mouth. Ask where the child rests and plays. Keep the area clean and free of small objects, sharp things like glass or stones, and heat such as fires, heaters, lamps and electric sockets; a mat that is shaken clean helps.

sections.title: Immunization: the schedule and checking status

read.text: Use the national schedule to decide which vaccines a child needs today.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Immunization is the most cost-effective way to reduce illness and death in children. Every child should complete the schedule before the first birthday. Check every child's status at every visit, and give missed vaccines that day. Too early, protection may not be adequate; late, the child is at risk.

AgeVaccines (Sudan national schedule)
BirthOPV 0, BCG
6 weeksOPV 1, Pentavalent 1, PCV 1, Rota 1, IPV 1
10 weeksOPV 2, Pentavalent 2, PCV 2, Rota 2
14 weeksOPV 3, Pentavalent 3, PCV 3, Rota 3, IPV 2
9 monthsMR, Men A, Yellow fever
18 monthsMR (booster)

Sudan national booklet: The national schedule adds IPV at 6 and 14 weeks, gives MR (measles-rubella), meningitis A and yellow fever at 9 months, and an MR booster at 18 months. Keep 4 weeks between doses of pentavalent, PCV, OPV and Rota, and 8 weeks between the IPV doses. WHO module (page 54): Birth BCG and OPV 0; 6, 10 and 14 weeks DPT-HepB-Hib (pentavalent), pneumococcal, rota and OPV; measles at 9 months. Repeated doses at least 4 weeks apart.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

cards.back: Not after 14 days of age: give OPV 1 at 6 weeks instead, with the other 6-week vaccines.
Not after 1 year of age.
At any age if not given before; over 1 year, only after a negative Mantoux test.
Give the OPV dose that is due, but do not count it; ask the mother to return in 4 weeks for an extra dose.

steps.title: Ask for the child health book
steps.text: Compare the dates with the schedule, and find the vaccines missed or due today.

steps.title: No book?
steps.text: Ask what the child has received. If you doubt the report, vaccinate. Give her a child health book to bring each time.

steps.title: Give and record
steps.text: Unless the child is being referred, give the vaccines today, record the dates, and write the return date.

read.text: Counsel on common reactions to vaccines, and vaccinate sick children unless there is a true contraindication.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: An adverse event following immunization (AEFI) is an unwanted event after a vaccine; it may be caused by the vaccine or happen by chance. Most are minor: low fever, pain, redness or swelling at the injection site, crying and irritability. Explain them at vaccination, so they do not keep the mother, or other mothers, away next time. Extensive swelling of the whole limb is not common: the child returns to the facility.
For fever over 38.5 °C after vaccination give paracetamol (15 mg/kg a dose), for up to 2 days. Do not give paracetamol at the time of vaccination.

cards.back: Common illness, including malnutrition. If a sick child is well enough to go home, vaccinate.
Do not give BCG to a child with HIV infection (AIDS).
Do not give it to a child who had convulsions (or shock) within 72 hours of the last dose, or who has a neurological disease.
If you refer the child, you need not vaccinate first; the hospital decides, so referral is not delayed.

read.text: Vaccinate today (if due)?

items.text: Will be treated at home with antibiotics
Has a local skin infection
Pentavalent 2 for a child who convulsed right after pentavalent 1
Older brother had a convulsion last year
Very low weight
BCG for a child known to have AIDS
Cough or cold

read.text: Also advise the mother to have the other children in the family vaccinated.
Give routine vitamin A and deworming at the right age and interval, and record them.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Vitamin A protects the eyes and the lining of the airways, gut and urinary tract, and helps resist severe infection. Deficiency is the leading cause of preventable blindness in children and increases deaths from measles, diarrhoea and pneumonia. Good vitamin A status at 6–59 months cuts measles deaths by half and diarrhoea deaths by a third.

AgeRoutine vitamin A
6 months up to 12 months100 000 IU (blue capsule)
12 months up to 5 years200 000 IU (red capsule)

Sudan national booklet: Give the first dose any time after 6 months, then every 6 months up to 5 years. Do not give it if a dose was given in the last 6 months or the child is on RUTF. Look for doses from campaigns on the child card. WHO module (page 60): The same schedule; the WHO table also allows several smaller capsules (for example 2 × 100 000 IU or 4 × 50 000 IU for 200 000 IU).
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: Cut the nipple of the capsule with a clean blade or scissors (or pierce it with a clean, new needle) and squeeze the contents into the child's mouth. Record the date: doses less than 6 months apart risk overdose.
Deworming

Roundworm, hookworm and whipworm cause loss of micronutrients, poor appetite, anaemia, poor growth and malnutrition. From 12 months, check at every visit whether the child had a deworming dose in the last 6 months; if not, give one.

Medicine, single dose every 6 months1 up to 2 years2 up to 5 years
Albendazole 400 mg tablet½ tablet (200 mg)1 tablet (400 mg)
Mebendazole 500 mg tablet½ tablet (250 mg)1 tablet (500 mg)
Chewable tablets are best. Under 3 years, crush the tablet between two spoons and add water. In the national chart booklet, mebendazole for a child with ANAEMIA is the syrup course in Module 6.
Sabrina (8 months), Angie (12 months, vitamin A 6 months ago), Jot (26 months, vitamin A 4 months ago, mebendazole 8 months ago):

items.text: Vitamin A for Sabrina
Mebendazole for Sabrina
Mebendazole for Angie
Vitamin A for Angie
Vitamin A for Jot
items.why: Less than 6 months since the last dose.

items.text: Mebendazole for Jot

read.text: Counsel families on preventing road injuries, drowning, burns, falls and poisoning.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Injuries are a growing problem in developing countries; nearly all are unintentional (accidents), and for every death many more children are left disabled. Ask about the home, where the child plays, how the child travels, how water is stored, and how the family cooks, heats and lights the home, then advise.

cards.back: Children do not play near the road; supervise play. Helmets on bicycles and motorcycles; seat belts or child seats in cars. Do not leave preschool children in the care of other children. Communities: pavements, safe playgrounds, speed limits.
Remove or cover toilet pits, wells and ponds; cover buckets and water drums; supervise children near any water, even a bath; flotation devices when swimming.

No playing with fire; raised, protected cooking areas with pot handles out of reach; do not hold the baby while cooking; supervise children by a fire; never leave children alone or locked in; no candle or kerosene lamp left lit while sleeping.
Guards on beds, stairs, windows and roofs; supervise children at play.

Keep medicines and poisons out of reach, in child-resistant packs and their original labelled containers. Never store kerosene or poisons in soda or water bottles. Do not send children to fetch or give medicines.

read.text: Safe or unsafe?

items.text: Kerosene kept in an old soda bottle
Cooking on a raised, enclosed stove
A lamp left lit while the family sleeps
The well is covered
A 5-year-old minds the baby by the road

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Pre-test
narrative: Before you begin studying this module, quickly practice your knowledge with the questions below. Do not look up the answers. This is for your own exercise. After you finish the module, you will answer the same questions. This will demonstrate to you what you have learned during the course of the module!

questions.question: If a child arrives at your clinic with a sign of serious illness, they should be immediately referred. What are these signs?
points: Child is lethargic or unconscious
Child is vomiting everything
Child has had convulsions, or is convulsing now
Child cannot breastfeed or drink
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.2 Checking all sick children.

questions.question: When is a child lethargic?
options: The child will not wake, even after shaking
The child is sleeping more often than usual, but will wake up if you set them down to walk
The child is drowsy and will not follow movement or noise in the room
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.2 Checking all sick children.

questions.question: When is a child unconscious?
options: The child will not wake, even after shaking. However, his eyes might be open.
The child is drowsy and will not follow movement or noise in the room
The child is sleeping very deeply
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.2 Checking all sick children.

questions.question: If you identify a child with serious illness that requires referral, your course of action is:
options: Stop your assessment of the child, and tell the caregiver they must hurry to the hospital
Provide urgent treatments, prepare the caregiver for travel to the hospital, and prepare supplies and a referral note
Keep the child at your clinic to monitor them and see if they will improve during the course of the day, and then refer only when necessary
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.3 Care when urgent referral is required.

questions.question: Why do some children require urgent referral?
options: The parents do not want to receive care in the clinic
It is quickest if the child receives important care at a different facility
They show signs of serious illness that require advanced care that is usually available at a referral facility, like a hospital.
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.2 and 1.3.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Exercise C (Salina, 15 months)
narrative: Salina is 15 months old. She weighs 8.5 kg. Her temperature is 38.5 °C.
The health worker asked, "What are the child's problems?" The mother said, "Salina has been coughing for 4 days, and she is not eating well."
This is Salina's initial visit for this problem.
The health worker checked Salina for general danger signs. He asked, "Is Salina able to drink or breastfeed?" The mother said, "No. Salina does not want to breastfeed."
The health worker gave Salina some water. She was too weak to lift her head. She was not able to drink from a cup.
Next he asked the mother, "Is she vomiting?" The mother said, "No."
Then he asked, "Has she had convulsions?" The mother said, "No."
The health worker looked to see if Salina was lethargic or unconscious. When the health worker and the mother were talking, Salina watched them and looked around the room.
learningPoints: Salina was not able to drink from a cup, so she has the general danger sign "not able to drink or breastfeed".
She watched the health worker and her mother and looked around the room, so she is not lethargic.
One general danger sign is enough: the danger sign is present, and Salina needs urgent referral.
exercises.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 25. Her problems: cough for 4 days, not eating well. Initial visit. Circle NOT ABLE TO DRINK OR BREASTFEED; danger sign present: Yes.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Lebo, 19 months (the module case)
narrative: Lebo's grandmother carries him into the clinic. Lebo does not look well. She has walked for one hour to the clinic. She tells you that she is also taking care of 4 other grandchildren. Lebo is her youngest grandchild and she is very worried about him. She says he is acting very unwell and has had a cough for 7 days.

She tells you this is the first time she is bringing Lebo in to the clinic. You ask her how old Lebo is. She says he is 19 months old. You ask Lebo's grandmother her name. She tells you that her name is Nthabeleng.

What is Lebo's problem? Nthabeleng tells you that Lebo has had a cough for 7 days. She also says that he has not been eating well. Nthabeleng is very worried about this. She says that in the past two days, he cannot take anything at all and she says he is very weak. This is concerning to you.

Is Lebo coming for an initial or follow-up visit? Nthabeleng told you that this is her first time bringing him to the clinic for this issue. This is an initial visit. Lebo's temperature and weight were recorded when he came into the clinic, he weighs 10 kg and his temperature is 37 Celsius.

You ask if Lebo is able to drink or breastfeed, and Nthabeleng says, "no, not today, he is too tired." You try to give him some water from a cup but he is too weak and does not swallow. You ask Nthabeleng if Lebo is vomiting, and she says "no." You ask if Lebo is having convulsions, and Nthabeleng says "no."

You look at Lebo's condition. He is not paying attention to you or Nthabeleng as you talk, and only stares ahead. You snap your fingers in front of his face, but he does not look at the fingers. You ask Nthabeleng to bounce Lebo and speak to him, and when she says "Lebo! Lebo!" he does not look up at her.
learningPoints: Lebo is showing two general danger signs - he is unable to drink and lethargic. He needs to be referred immediately to the hospital.
exercises.explain: Lebo is showing two general danger signs - he is unable to drink and lethargic. He needs to be referred immediately to the hospital.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Exercise D (true or false)
narrative: What will you do for the children who have general danger signs? Which statements below are true, and which are false?
When you check your answers, the true version of each false statement is shown.

questions.question: Stop immediately and send the child to the hospital
questions.explain: The true statement: Continue the assessment quickly, identify all pre-referral treatments needed, treat, and refer urgently. Answer key: Module 1, page 25.

questions.question: Continue the assessment, determine pre-referral treatment, treat, and refer.
questions.explain: True. Answer key: Module 1, page 25.

questions.question: Continue to assess the child and send child to hospital with referral note about all of the treatments you identified.
questions.explain: The true statement: You should deliver the necessary pre-referral treatment before they leave your clinic for the hospital. Answer key: Module 1, page 25.

questions.question: If referral is not possible, there is nothing you can do. Send the child home.
questions.explain: The true statement: You can provide essential care (further discussed in Annex), work with the family to encourage them to go to the hospital, or bring the child near to the clinic to monitor treatment and progress. Answer key: Module 1, page 25.

narrative: Below are questions about the module. You are allowed to use your Chart Booklet as you answer these questions. You should not use your study modules.

questions.question: According to IMCI charts, a sick child is:
options: 2 months up to 5 years of age

options: Take the child and examine him
Greet the caregiver to make her feel welcome

questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

Age, weight, temperature, child's problem according to caregiver, and if the visit is initial or follow-up
Why the caregiver came to the clinic

questions.question: How do you check if a child is unable to breastfeed or drink?
options: You can tell by looking because the child will be small

options: He is drowsy and is not alert or awake. He will not show interest in what is happening around him, he only stares ahead.

He will respond once you speak or clap.

questions.question: If a child is unconscious, how does he look and act?
options: His eyes follow your hand if you wave in front of his face.

questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

Counsel the mother on home treatment and feeding

No pre-referral treatment needed, send the child immediately to the hospital to not delay.
Pre-referral treatments are listed in bold type in the classification tables. Give all pre-referral treatments for all classifications.
