questions.question: If a child has a general danger sign, stop the assessment immediately and send them to the hospital.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: If referral is not possible, there is not much you can do, so you should send the child home.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: IMCI for the sick child and young infant are exactly the same.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Pre-test
narrative: Before you begin studying this module, check what you know. Do not look up the answers. After the module you will answer the same questions.

questions.question: Why do young infants require different care than sick children?
options: Young infants are much quicker to recover from illness because they are young.
Young infants show signs of illness differently. They can also become ill and die from an infection very quickly.
Young infants very rarely get sick.
questions.explain: Introduction to the sick young infant: young infants are special.

questions.question: Which of the following is important care for a young infant?
options: Keeping the infant loosely bundled so he can begin to move his arms and legs
Keeping the umbilical cord moist so that it falls off quickly
Keeping the infant warm through skin-to-skin care
questions.explain: Introduction and infant care lessons: keep the infant warm; the cord is kept clean and dry.

questions.question: What are the feeding recommendations for sick young infants?
options: Exclusive, on-demand breastfeeding for at least 6 months
Breastfeeding and additional sources of fluid, like water, to hydrate
Soft complementary foods as soon as the child is ready
questions.explain: Feeding lessons: exclusive, on-demand breastfeeding. (The printed WHO answer key gives B, which contradicts the module text.)

questions.question: What are signs that a young infant is seriously ill and needs urgent referral and care?
options: Breathing more than 60 breaths per minute
Some jaundice, where the eyes are yellow but not the palms or soles
questions.explain: Signs of serious disease: fast breathing (60 or more, counted twice) is a sign of very severe disease. A few pustules are a local infection.

questions.question: A young infant presents at your clinic. The caregiver says the infant had been feeding well, but in the past 2 days is unable to breastfeed at all. What actions will you take?
options: Counsel the caregiver on positioning and attachment so that the infant can breastfeed better.
The infant is seriously ill if they are unable to feed. You must urgently refer.
Recommend that the caregiver give other safe fluids by cup.
questions.explain: Signs of serious disease and feeding lessons: not able to feed is a severe sign.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise A (young infants are special)
narrative: Try not to look back at the material.

questions.question: Young infants are up to 2 months of age.
Young infants have a different section of charts because they have a separate IMNCI process that is entirely different from the process for the sick child.
questions.explain: The process is the same; the charts are separate because some signs and symptoms are age-specific.

questions.question: Severe infections are the most serious illness in the first two months of life.
Young infants and children are very similar in how they show signs of illness.
questions.explain: Young infants show signs of illness very differently, so they are assessed for different signs and symptoms.

questions.question: Sami is 2 months old. He is considered a sick young infant.
questions.explain: At 2 months Sami is a sick child: young infants are up to 2 months.

questions.question: Tick the measures that are important care for young infants.
options: Skin-to-skin contact (kangaroo care) to keep the infant warm
Give water regularly to keep infant hydrated
Seek care immediately if infant develops signs of serious illness
Change gowns before holding young infant
Give all immunizations at birth, and never again
Wash hands before handling the young infant
Rub the young infant with oils, lotion, or vaseline to keep skin moist

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise B (signs of serious illness)
narrative: Answer the questions about assessing for signs of serious illness.

questions.question: How many breaths per minute is fast breathing in a young infant?
How do you decide if an infant has fast breathing?
points: Make sure the infant is calm
Count the breaths in one minute
If 60 or more, count a second time to confirm

questions.question: How will you measure temperature in a young infant?
points: Axillary (armpit) temperature
Or feel the infant's abdomen or armpit
Rectal thresholds are about 0.5 °C higher

questions.question: What temperature is a fever in a young infant?
What temperature is low body temperature?
Chest indrawing is identified when an infant is breathing OUT.
questions.explain: It is seen when the infant breathes IN: the lower chest wall goes in instead of out.

questions.question: A healthy umbilicus is often red, and sometimes drains pus.
questions.explain: A red or draining umbilicus is a sign of infection.

questions.question: Any difficulty with feeding is an important issue for young infants.
Only severe chest indrawing is a serious sign in infants, as mild chest indrawing is normal in young infants.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise C (jaundice)
narrative: Answer the questions about assessing and classifying jaundice.

questions.question: Jaundice is a yellow discolouration of the skin.
Yellow soles and palms are normal in young infants.
questions.explain: Yellow palms and soles mean SEVERE JAUNDICE.

questions.question: Many babies may have jaundice in the first week of life, especially if they are low birth weight or premature.
Jaundice in a young infant less than 24 hours old is very serious.
To assess for jaundice of the skin, soles or palms, blanch the skin and look for discolouration.
It is best to look for jaundice indoors under a lamp.
questions.explain: Look in natural light.

questions.question: Jaundice that persists beyond 2 weeks requires further investigation.
Precious is 14 days old. Her skin is not discoloured. Her palms and soles are normal.
Kai was born last night, less than 24 hours ago. His skin is very yellow.
Sal is 2 weeks old. She has yellow discolouration of the skin and eyes. Her palms and soles are not yellow.
questions.explain: JAUNDICE. At 14 days or older she should also be referred for assessment.

questions.question: Biki is 21 days old. He has yellow skin, but his palms and soles are not yellow. How would you classify Biki? What would you do?
points: JAUNDICE (yellow)
He is older than 14 days: refer for assessment

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise D, Henri (6 hours)
narrative: Henri was born 6 hours ago at home. His weight is 3.0 kg. His axillary temperature is 36.5 °C. He is brought to the health facility because he did not cry immediately after birth and is having difficult breathing.
The health worker first checks the young infant for signs of very severe disease and local bacterial infection. The father says that the young infant has not had convulsions and has not yet been fed.

The health worker counts 74 breaths per minute. He repeats the count: the second count is 70 breaths per minute. He finds that the young infant has severe chest indrawing. The young infant moves only when he is stimulated. The umbilicus is normal, and there are no skin pustules.
There is no jaundice. Henri does not have diarrhoea.
learningPoints: Henri has fast breathing (counted twice), severe chest indrawing and moves only when stimulated: POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE (red). He needs urgent referral.
exercises.explain: Henri has fast breathing (counted twice), severe chest indrawing and moves only when stimulated: POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE (red). He needs urgent referral.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise D, Sashi (1 week)
narrative: Sashi is 1 week old. Her weight is 3.4 kg. Her axillary temperature is 37 °C. Her caregiver brought her to the clinic because she has a rash.
The health worker assesses for signs of very severe disease and local bacterial infection. Sashi's caregiver says that there were no convulsions and that the infant is feeding well.

Sashi's breathing rate is 55 per minute. She has no chest indrawing. Her umbilicus is normal. The health worker examines her entire body and finds a red rash with a few skin pustules on her buttocks. She is awake and has spontaneous movements.
She has neither jaundice nor diarrhoea.
learningPoints: A few skin pustules with no sign of very severe disease: LOCAL BACTERIAL INFECTION (yellow). Treat at home and follow up in 2 days.
exercises.explain: A few skin pustules with no sign of very severe disease: LOCAL BACTERIAL INFECTION (yellow). Treat at home and follow up in 2 days.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Mimi, 6 weeks (the module case)
narrative: Biya brings her first child, Mimi, aged 6 weeks, on Tuesday morning. Since the weekend Mimi has not been taking the breast as often as usual, and Biya thinks she is getting worse. This is the first visit for this problem.
Mimi weighs 3.1 kg (birth weight 3.5 kg). Her axillary temperature is 34.7 °C.
Biya tries several times to put Mimi on the breast but Mimi does not attach at all. Biya says that she has had no convulsions.

You count 45 breaths per minute. Her lower chest wall moves in quite severely when she breathes in. She has no skin pustules. The umbilicus is not red or draining pus. When you move Mimi's arm to stimulate her, she drops the arm when you release it.
When you press Mimi's skin in natural light it is yellow, and her palms and soles are also yellow. Biya is not sure when the yellow colour first appeared.
learningPoints: Mimi has four signs of very severe disease (not feeding well, low body temperature, severe chest indrawing, reduced movement) and yellow palms and soles. Two red classifications: refer urgently after the first dose of ampicillin and gentamicin, preventing low blood sugar and keeping her warm.
exercises.explain: Mimi has four signs of very severe disease (not feeding well, low body temperature, severe chest indrawing, reduced movement) and yellow palms and soles. Two red classifications: refer urgently after the first dose of ampicillin and gentamicin, preventing low blood sugar and keeping her warm.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise E (treatment for Henri and Sashi)
narrative: Return to Henri's and Sashi's recording forms. Decide the treatments, using the young infant chart (Sudan national booklet doses). Write complete answers including the schedule and dose.

questions.question: Henri should be urgently referred.
questions.explain: He is classified POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE.

questions.question: Henri is 6 hours old and weighs 3.0 kg. What pre-referral treatments does he need?
points: First dose of IM ampicillin 1.5 ml (250 mg/2.5 ml)
First dose of IM gentamicin 1.5 ml (10 mg/ml, under 7 days)
Treat to prevent low blood sugar (breastfeed, or 30 ml breast milk or sugar water, by tube if he cannot swallow)
Advise how to keep him warm on the way
Refer urgently
questions.explain: Sudan booklet doses. The WHO module gives ampicillin 1.0 ml and gentamicin 1.6 ml for its formulations.

questions.question: Sashi should be urgently referred.
questions.explain: Sashi has LOCAL BACTERIAL INFECTION and is treated at home.

questions.question: Sashi is 1 week old and weighs 3.4 kg. What treatments and advice does she need?
points: Oral amoxicillin 2.5 ml syrup (125 mg/5 ml) or ¼ tablet (250 mg) twice daily for 5 days; first dose in the clinic
Teach the caregiver to give it at home, with checking questions
Teach her to treat the pustules: wash hands, wash off pus and crusts with soap and water, dry, paint with gentian violet 0.5%, wash hands; twice daily for 5 days
Follow up in 2 days
Signs to return immediately
questions.explain: Sudan uses amoxicillin. The WHO module also allows co-trimoxazole 1.25 ml syrup twice daily.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise F (follow-up for Sashi)
narrative: Sashi, 1 week old, was classified LOCAL BACTERIAL INFECTION for skin pustules on her buttocks. Her caregiver gave the oral antibiotic and learned to clean the skin and apply gentian violet. She returns after 2 days with no new problems.

questions.question: How would you reassess Sashi?
points: Look at the skin pustules: are there many or severe pustules?
Are the redness and pus improved: fewer pustules, drying up?

questions.question: You see fewer pustules and less redness. What does Sashi need now?
options: Complete the 5 days of antibiotic, and continue cleaning and gentian violet for 5 days
Stop the antibiotic: she is better
questions.explain: She is improving, but must finish the 5 days of treatment.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise G (feeding and weight for age)
narrative: Practise assessing feeding. For the weight questions, use the young infant weight-for-age chart in your chart booklet.

questions.question: What are three very important recommendations about the best way to feed a young infant from 0 to 6 months?
points: Exclusive: only breast milk, no other food or fluids
On demand: whenever the infant wants, day and night
At least 8 times in 24 hours

questions.question: A young infant with severe jaundice should be assessed for feeding problems and low weight.
questions.explain: A severe (red) classification is referred urgently, so the feeding and weight assessment is skipped.

questions.question: 2.5 kg at 1 month: is this infant low weight for age?
3 kg at 2 weeks: is this infant low weight for age?
4 kg at 8 weeks: is this infant low weight for age?
3.2 kg at 4 weeks: is this infant low weight for age?
4.5 kg at 3 weeks: is this infant low weight for age?
3.3 kg at 2 weeks: is this infant low weight for age?
3.1 kg at 7 weeks: is this infant low weight for age?
What is low birth weight?
What is very low birth weight?

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercises H and I (attachment and suckling)
narrative: Decide whether each sign shows good or poor attachment, then match each infant with how well they are suckling.

questions.question: Chin away from breast
More areola visible above than below mouth
Narrow mouth with lips pushed forward
Equal amount areola visible below/above mouth
Mouth wide open
Lower lip turned outward
Chin touching breast
Lower lip turned in
Unable to suck breast milk. Nose is not blocked.
Suckles deeply, sometimes pausing. Releases on own when satisfied.
Rapid, shallow sucks. Cannot hear swallowing. Cheeks draw in. Restless.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise J (immunizations)
narrative: Decide if the infant needs any immunizations today, and which ones, using the national schedule (birth: OPV 0, BCG; 6 weeks: OPV 1, Rota 1, PCV 1, Penta 1, IPV 1; 10 weeks: OPV 2, Rota 2, PCV 2, Penta 2).

questions.question: 16 days old, received BCG.
questions.explain: OPV 0 is not given after 14 days. Give the 6-week vaccines at 6 weeks.

questions.question: 7 weeks old, received Penta 1 (WHO: DPT-1 and Hib-1). What does the infant need today?
points: OPV 1
Rota 1, PCV 1 and IPV 1 if not given
Next appointment at 10 weeks
questions.explain: WHO answer: OPV 1 and hepatitis B 1. In Sudan, hepatitis B is part of Penta.

questions.question: 4 weeks old, received BCG and OPV 0.
8 weeks old, received BCG and OPV 0. The infant is being urgently referred today.
options: No vaccines now; refer urgently and note the vaccines due on the referral note
Give all the 6-week vaccines first, then refer
questions.explain: Do not immunize before referral.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise K (counselling on feeding)
narrative: Practise counselling a caregiver about infant feeding.

questions.question: Spoon feeding is not safe.
questions.explain: Spoon feeding is safe if the mother gives enough, though slower than a cup.

questions.question: Cup feeding is the preferred method of feeding (when an infant cannot breastfeed).
Bottle feeding is unsafe.
Cup feeding is preferred over spoon feeding.
Bottle feeding is most recommended for young infants to practise suckling.
Srilekha is unsure how to hold her infant while breastfeeding. How will you show her?
points: Head and body in line
Facing the breast, nose opposite the nipple
Held close to her body
Whole body supported, not just the neck and shoulders

questions.question: Yoonhee is unsure how to help her infant attach. What should she do?
points: Touch the infant's lips with her nipple
Wait until the mouth is opening wide
Move the infant quickly onto the breast, aiming the lower lip well below the nipple

questions.question: How often should a caregiver breastfeed in 24 hours?
Jaya breastfeeds but also gives her 4-month-old some watery porridge. What do you recommend?
points: Breastfeed more: on demand, at least 8 times in 24 hours
Stop the porridge and breastfeed exclusively
Find out why she began the porridge and what feeding difficulties she has

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise L (home care for Sashi)
narrative: Use Sashi's case: local bacterial infection with pustules on her buttocks.

questions.question: List the steps the caregiver should take to treat the skin pustules at home.
points: Wash hands
Gently wash off pus and crusts with soap and water
Dry the area
Paint with gentian violet (0.5%)
Wash hands

questions.question: How often should she treat the pustules?
What are the 3 main points of home care for the young infant?
points: Breastfeed frequently, as often and as long as the infant wants, day and night
When to return
Keep the young infant warm at all times

questions.question: What would you tell Sashi's caregiver about when to return?
points: Follow-up in 2 days to check the pustules are improving
Return immediately if breastfeeding poorly, sicker, fever, fast or difficult breathing, feels cold, yellow palms and soles

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Review questions (post-test)
narrative: You have finished the module. Answer the same questions as in the pre-test and compare your scores.

questions.question: Why do young infants require different care than sick children?
options: Young infants are much quicker to recover from illness because they are young.
Young infants show signs of illness differently. They can also become ill and die from an infection very quickly.
Young infants very rarely get sick.
questions.explain: Introduction to the sick young infant: young infants are special.

questions.question: Which of the following is important care for a young infant?
options: Keeping the infant loosely bundled so he can begin to move his arms and legs
Keeping the umbilical cord moist so that it falls off quickly
Keeping the infant warm through skin-to-skin care
questions.explain: Introduction and infant care lessons: keep the infant warm; the cord is kept clean and dry.

questions.question: What are the feeding recommendations for sick young infants?
options: Exclusive, on-demand breastfeeding for at least 6 months
Breastfeeding and additional sources of fluid, like water, to hydrate
Soft complementary foods as soon as the child is ready
questions.explain: Feeding lessons: exclusive, on-demand breastfeeding. (The printed WHO answer key gives B, which contradicts the module text.)

questions.question: What are signs that a young infant is seriously ill and needs urgent referral and care?
options: Breathing more than 60 breaths per minute
Some jaundice, where the eyes are yellow but not the palms or soles
questions.explain: Signs of serious disease: fast breathing (60 or more, counted twice) is a sign of very severe disease. A few pustules are a local infection.

questions.question: A young infant presents at your clinic. The caregiver says the infant had been feeding well, but in the past 2 days is unable to breastfeed at all. What actions will you take?
options: Counsel the caregiver on positioning and attachment so that the infant can breastfeed better.
The infant is seriously ill if they are unable to feed. You must urgently refer.
Recommend that the caregiver give other safe fluids by cup.
questions.explain: Signs of serious disease and feeding lessons: not able to feed is a severe sign.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Logbook assessment questions
narrative: Questions about the module. You may use your chart booklet, but not your study modules.

questions.question: In IMNCI, the sick young infant refers to:
Which of these is a sign of very severe disease in a young infant?
options: Chest indrawing, either mild or severe

questions.question: Which of these is a sign of local bacterial infection in a young infant?
options: 3 skin pustules on the infant's shoulder

questions.question: A 2-week-old has fast breathing if he is breathing:
options: 50 breaths per minute or more, counted twice
60 breaths or more per minute, and the same in a second count

questions.question: A 7-week-old classified with very severe disease:
options: Should be assessed for correct position and attachment for breastfeeding
Can improve at the clinic level and does not need urgent referral
Needs a first dose of IM antibiotics before urgent referral

questions.question: A 1-month-old with diarrhoea can be classified SEVERE DEHYDRATION if:
options: The child had very low weight for age
The child was lethargic even though there was no other sign of dehydration
The child had at least two signs of dehydration

questions.question: Thato is 14 days old. His palms appear yellow. How do you classify, and what will you do?
options: SEVERE JAUNDICE, treat Thato in the clinic
JAUNDICE, and refer if Thato returns after 1 week with jaundice

questions.question: An infant has good attachment if:
options: His lower lip is turned in and more areola is visible below than above the mouth
The chin is touching the breast and his lower lip is turned outward
More areola shows above the mouth and his mouth is narrow

questions.question: An infant may not suckle effectively if:
options: Her mouth is wide open when she is attached
She is taking slow, deep sucks
She has a blocked nose or is classified with very severe disease

questions.question: If an infant has a feeding problem, this could mean he is:
options: Not well attached, having less than 8 breastfeeds in 24 hours, or receiving other foods or drinks
Receiving only breast milk from the mother, and feeding on demand
Receiving expressed breast milk from a cup

questions.question: An infant who is 2 months old is a young infant.
A young infant brought to the clinic because of difficulty feeding can be treated by the clinic nurse.
questions.explain: Not feeding well is a sign of very severe disease: refer urgently.

questions.question: A young infant with cough or difficult breathing and severe chest indrawing is classified as SEVERE PNEUMONIA.
questions.explain: In the young infant, severe chest indrawing is a sign of very severe disease.

questions.question: If a young infant is brought in while convulsing, rush the baby to hospital and do not spend time giving treatments.
questions.explain: Give the pre-referral treatments (Sudan: manage the airway and give rectal diazepam; first dose of antibiotics) then refer.

questions.question: A young infant aged 6 weeks with jaundice may have a serious problem and needs to be referred to a hospital.
questions.explain: Jaundice at 14 days or older: refer for assessment (Sudan and WHO charts). The printed WHO key says FALSE: reviewer to confirm.

questions.question: A young infant with severe chest indrawing can be classified with very severe disease.
Umbilicus care and good hygiene are very important to keeping a young infant healthy.
One important sign of good attachment is that the infant's mouth is wide open.
You need to give the young infant water frequently to prevent dehydration.
questions.explain: Exclusive breastfeeding: no water.

questions.question: Skin-to-skin contact keeps an infant warm.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 3: Pre-test
narrative: Before you begin studying this module, check what you know. After the module you will answer the same questions.

questions.question: What clinical signs can help you identify if a child has pneumonia?
If a child has pneumonia, how will you treat?
Why is it important to correctly identify and manage pneumonia?
options: Pneumonia is very common, but it is not so serious for children
Pneumonia is a major killer of children under 5 around the world, and it requires early management
Children with pneumonia need to be isolated from all other family members

questions.question: Chest indrawing is when:
options: The lower ribs move in when the child breathes out
The lower ribs move in when the child breathes in
The lower ribs are always pushed in, no matter if the child is breathing in or out

questions.question: Children who have a cough, but do not show signs of pneumonia, should immediately receive an antibiotic.
questions.explain: A child with COUGH OR COLD does not need an antibiotic.

questions.question: The following is a good checking question: "How will you prepare a safe home remedy for cough?"
questions.explain: It cannot be answered with yes or no.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 3: Exercise A (assess)
narrative: Practise what you have learned about assessing cough or difficult breathing.

questions.question: Which two clinical signs help you identify children with pneumonia?
A child of 3 years with 36 breaths per minute has fast breathing.
questions.explain: From 12 months up to 5 years, fast breathing is 40 or more.

questions.question: A child of 12 months with 50 breaths per minute has fast breathing.
questions.explain: From 12 months up to 5 years, fast breathing is 40 or more.

questions.question: A child of 6 months with 45 breaths per minute has fast breathing.
questions.explain: From 2 months up to 12 months, fast breathing is 50 or more.

questions.question: A child of 3 months with 57 breaths per minute has fast breathing.
questions.explain: From 2 months up to 12 months, fast breathing is 50 or more.

questions.question: Julie arrives at your clinic with her mother. You gather the important information and check Julie for danger signs: she has none. What do you ASK and LOOK for next?
points: ASK: does the child have cough or difficult breathing?
LOOK: do you notice any issues with breathing?

questions.question: Julie's mother says Julie has no cough or difficult breathing. You watch Julie, and she seems to be breathing regularly. What do you do next?
options: Continue to the next assessment, for diarrhoea
Count her breaths in one minute

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 3: Exercise B (classify)
narrative: Open your chart booklet and review the classification table for cough or difficult breathing.

questions.question: Sal is 9 months old and has a cough. You count 45 breaths per minute. No chest indrawing or stridor.
options: SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE
questions.explain: 45 is not fast breathing under 12 months (the cut-off is 50), and there are no other signs.

questions.question: Linus is 3 months old, and you count 65 breaths in one minute. He has had convulsions during the current illness.
options: SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE
questions.explain: Convulsions during this illness are a general danger sign.

questions.question: Jojo is 3 years old. You count 56 breaths in one minute. No indrawing or stridor.
options: SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE
questions.explain: 56 is fast breathing from 12 months (the cut-off is 40).

questions.question: You should look for chest indrawing when the child breathes OUT.
questions.explain: You look for chest indrawing when the child breathes IN.

questions.question: Fast breathing in a child 12 months and older is 40 or more a minute.
Chest indrawing is a sign of pneumonia.
If a child has a cough but no other signs, they probably have pneumonia.
questions.explain: A child who shows no signs is classified as COUGH OR COLD.

questions.question: A child with chest indrawing will always also have fast breathing.
questions.explain: A child with chest indrawing may not have fast breathing.

questions.question: Chest indrawing is when the lower ribs move IN when the child breathes IN.
A child 2 up to 12 months has fast breathing if more than 45 breaths a minute.
questions.explain: Fast breathing in this age group is 50 or more breaths per minute.

questions.question: A child with chest indrawing has a higher risk of death from pneumonia than a child with fast breathing and no chest indrawing.
Difficult breathing can also be described as noisy, interrupted or fast.
If a child has cough, fast breathing and vomits everything, he is classified as PNEUMONIA (yellow).
questions.explain: Classify as SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE. Fast breathing is a sign of PNEUMONIA (yellow), but vomiting everything is a general danger sign (red). When a child has signs from different rows, you always classify with the more severe.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 3: Exercise C (Gyatsu, 6 months)
narrative: Gyatsu is 6 months old and weighs 5.5 kg. His temperature is 38 °C. His mother said he has had cough for 2 days.

The health worker checked for general danger signs. The mother said that Gyatsu is able to breastfeed. He has not vomited during this illness. He has not had convulsions. Gyatsu is not lethargic or unconscious.
The health worker said to the mother, "I want to check Gyatsu's cough. You said he has had cough for 2 days now. I am going to count his breaths. He will need to remain calm while I do this."
The health worker counted 58 breaths per minute. He did not see chest indrawing or hear stridor.
learningPoints: Gyatsu has no general danger sign and no stridor when calm, so he does not have the severe (red) classification.
58 breaths per minute is fast breathing at 6 months (the cut-off is 50).
Fast breathing with no red sign is classified PNEUMONIA (yellow).
exercises.explain: Gyatsu has no general danger sign and no stridor when calm, so he does not have the severe (red) classification. 58 breaths per minute is fast breathing at 6 months (the cut-off is 50). Fast breathing with no red sign is classified PNEUMONIA (yellow).

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 3: Exercise D (treatment)
narrative: Answer the questions about the treatments you have read about. Use the dosage table for amoxicillin.

questions.question: You should give a child the first-line antibiotic, unless it is unavailable or the child has not responded to it.
If a child has more than one illness that requires antibiotics, if possible, give one antibiotic for more than one illness.
If a child can drink, it is preferable to give an oral antibiotic.
If a child has two illnesses that require the same antibiotic, you should double the dose or give the treatment for 10 days instead of 5.
questions.explain: Do not double the size of each dose or give the antibiotic for a longer period.

questions.question: How often should you give amoxicillin for pneumonia?
A child is 3 months old, weighs 5 kg and can drink. You have amoxicillin syrup (250 mg/5 ml).
options: 5 ml, two times a day, for five days
10 ml, two times a day, for five days
2.5 ml, two times a day, for five days

questions.question: A child is 9 months old, and you have amoxicillin tablets (250 mg).
options: 1 tablet, two times a day, for five days
2 tablets, two times a day, for five days
½ tablet, two times a day, for five days

questions.question: A child is 13 months old and you do not know her weight. She can drink. You have amoxicillin syrup (250 mg/5 ml).
options: 5 ml, two times a day, for five days
10 ml, two times a day, for five days
15 ml, two times a day, for five days
questions.explain: 12 months up to 3 years: 10 ml.

questions.question: A child is 4 years old. You have amoxicillin tablets (250 mg).
options: 2 tablets, two times a day, for five days
3 tablets, two times a day, for five days
1 tablet, two times a day, for five days

questions.question: What is meant by a "safe" remedy? Give an example.
points: Remedies can be homemade, given at the clinic or bought at a pharmacy
Safe remedies are locally specific and recorded in your chart booklet
Breast milk is the best remedy for an exclusively breastfed child: do not give other drinks or remedies

questions.question: Give at least 2 examples of remedies that are not safe.
points: Remedies containing atropine
Remedies containing codeine or codeine derivatives
Remedies containing alcohol
Medicated nose drops (anything other than salt)
questions.explain: They may sedate the child, interfere with feeding, and interfere with the child's ability to cough up secretions from the lungs.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 3: Exercise E (checking questions)
narrative: Rewrite each question as a good checking question. A good checking question is open-ended: it begins with how, what, why, when or where, and cannot be answered yes or no.

questions.question: Do you remember when to give the amoxicillin?
points: For example: When will you give the amoxicillin?

questions.question: Do you understand how much amoxicillin syrup to give your child?
points: For example: How much syrup will you give your child?

questions.question: Did the nurse explain to you how to use an inhaler?
points: For example: How will you give the inhaler?

questions.question: Do you know how to make a remedy for the throat?
points: For example: How will you make a remedy for the throat at home?

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 3: Exercise F (counsel)
narrative: Nurse Aluka gives some oral antibiotics to a mother for her child, Maria Balana. Before he explains how to give them, Aluka asks the mother if she knows how to give her child the medicine. The mother nods her head yes. So Aluka gives her the antibiotics and says good-bye.

questions.question: If a mother tells you that she already knows how to give a treatment, what should you do?
points: Ask her to show you how to measure the dose, and to tell you the schedule for the antibiotic
If she is incorrect, give her the information and demonstrate
If she measures the dose correctly, ask her to give the first dose so you can observe

questions.question: Maria Balana is 4 months old and is classified PNEUMONIA. You have amoxicillin tablets (250 mg). What do you write on the drug label?
options: Amoxicillin, 10 tablets: give 1 tablet, two times a day, for 5 days
Amoxicillin, 5 tablets: give 1 tablet once a day for 5 days
Amoxicillin, 20 tablets: give 2 tablets, two times a day, for 5 days
questions.explain: 2 months up to 12 months: 1 tablet (250 mg) twice daily for 5 days, so 10 tablets in all.

questions.question: When should a child classified as COUGH OR COLD return immediately to the clinic?
options: If breathing becomes fast or difficult
If the child is still coughing after 2 days
Only if the mother runs out of the remedy

questions.question: When should the child come back for follow-up of the cough or cold?
options: In 5 days, only if the cough is not improving

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 3: Exercise G (Pandit's follow-up)
narrative: Pandit's mother has brought him back for follow-up. He is one year old. Three days ago he was classified as having PNEUMONIA and you gave him amoxicillin. You ask how he is doing and if he has developed any new problems. His mother says that he is much better.

questions.question: How would you reassess Pandit today? List all the signs you would look at and the questions you would ask his mother.
points: Is he able to drink or breastfeed?
Does he vomit everything?
Has he had convulsions?
See if he is lethargic or unconscious
Is he still coughing? How long has he been coughing?
Count the breaths in one minute
Look for chest indrawing
Look and listen for stridor
Is he breathing slower?
Is there less fever?
Is he eating better?

questions.question: Pandit has no general danger signs. He is still coughing, and has now been coughing for about 10 days. He is breathing 38 breaths per minute and has no chest indrawing and no stridor. He does not have fever. He is breastfeeding well and eating some food: he was refusing all food before. He was playing with his brother this morning. What actions will you take?
options: Tell his mother he is improving, and that she should continue the antibiotic until the 5 days are finished
questions.explain: Tell his mother that he is improving nicely. She should continue giving the medicine as she has been until it is all gone. Ask checking questions about how she has been giving the treatment, and address any concerns.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 3: Review questions (post-test)
narrative: Now that you have finished the module, answer the same questions as before.

questions.question: What clinical signs can help you identify if a child has pneumonia?
If a child has pneumonia, how will you treat?
Why is it important to correctly identify and manage pneumonia?
options: Pneumonia is very common, but it is not so serious for children
Pneumonia is a major killer of children under 5 around the world, and it requires early management
Children with pneumonia need to be isolated from all other family members

questions.question: Chest indrawing is when:
options: The lower ribs move in when the child breathes out
The lower ribs move in when the child breathes in
The lower ribs are always pushed in, no matter if the child is breathing in or out

questions.question: Children who have a cough, but do not show signs of pneumonia, should immediately receive an antibiotic.
questions.explain: A child with COUGH OR COLD does not need an antibiotic.

questions.question: The following is a good checking question: "How will you prepare a safe home remedy for cough?"
questions.explain: It cannot be answered with yes or no.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 3: Logbook assessment questions
narrative: You are allowed to use your chart booklet as you answer these questions. You should not use your study modules.

questions.question: When using IMNCI, what clinical signs help identify pneumonia?
options: Chest indrawing and blood when coughing

questions.question: A child is classified with SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE when which of the following signs is present:
options: Stridor when the child is calm

questions.question: Raj is 7 months old. He has fast breathing if:
Chest indrawing is when:
options: The lower ribs move in when the child breathes out.
The lower ribs move in when the child breathes in.
The lower ribs are always pushed in, no matter when the child is breathing in or out.

questions.question: Poorvaja is 3 years old. She has fast breathing if:
What is stridor?
options: A wheezing noise when the child breathes out
A wet noise when the child is sitting still and breathing
A harsh noise, caused by swelling, heard when the child breathes in

questions.question: Ntebo is 12 months old. He has fast breathing if:
Roma is 3 months old. You count 57 breaths in one minute. You do not hear stridor. When Roma breathes in, his lower ribs move in. How would you classify Roma's cough?
Which of the following are good teaching steps when explaining home treatment for a cough?
options: Give the caregiver some printed information and send the treatment home
Ask questions like "Will you give this medicine correctly?"
Explain how to give treatment, demonstrate giving treatment, and ask the caregiver to practise while you give feedback

questions.question: If the child has had a cough for more than 3 weeks, what steps should be taken?
options: Refer for TB or asthma assessment
Send the child home with a soothing remedy

questions.question: When giving antibiotics using IMNCI, it is important to consider all four of these issues: schedule, dosage, combining treatment if more than one illness can be treated with a single antibiotic, and only using the second-line medicines if the first line is not available or the child did not respond to the first line.
You will only assess a child for a cough or difficult breathing if the caregiver specifically says that cough is the reason they came to the clinic.
A child with a cough but no signs of pneumonia can be treated at home.
Oral antibiotics are given to children with pneumonia.
It is best to count breaths for fast breathing when the child is active and moving around.
If a child has fast breathing and no other signs, they are classified PNEUMONIA.
A child with chest indrawing can be treated in the clinic.
A child with PNEUMONIA should return to the clinic in 2 days.
questions.explain: Follow up in 3 days.

questions.question: If a child with pneumonia returns for follow-up and has not improved, and they have been receiving the first-line antibiotic correctly, start the second-line antibiotic if it is available.
Pneumonia and other acute respiratory infections are major killers of children worldwide.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Pre-test
narrative: Before you begin studying this module, check what you know. After the module you will answer the same questions.

questions.question: How can diarrhoea kill children?
options: Children lose valuable fluids, salts and sugars, which can cause shock to vital organs
Children lose valuable nutrients because they cannot eat

questions.question: What are critical treatments for children with diarrhoea and dehydration?
What is persistent diarrhoea?
options: When a child frequently has diarrhoea over a period of 1 month, and is ill as a result
When a child has several episodes of diarrhoea a day
When a child has an episode of diarrhoea lasting 14 days or more, which is particularly dangerous for dehydration and malnutrition

questions.question: Critical messages for caregivers about diarrhoea and dehydration include:
options: The child must receive increased fluids, ORS, zinc and regular feeding
The child requires ORS, but should receive less food in order to reduce the diarrhoea
The child should immediately receive antibiotics to stop the diarrhoea

questions.question: Nidhi arrives at your clinic and is very lethargic. Her eyes are very sunken. She has diarrhoea. You observe a significant loss of skin elasticity. How will you manage Nidhi?
options: Nidhi requires ORS immediately, as she is dehydrated
These are common signs of diarrhoea, as the child's body is exhausted
Nidhi is severely dehydrated. She requires urgent rehydration therapy by IV or nasogastric tube

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Exercise A (Maya, 25 months)
narrative: Maya is at the clinic today because she has had diarrhoea for 4 days. She is 25 months old. She weighs 9 kg. Her temperature is 37.0 °C.
Maya has no general danger signs. She does not have cough or difficult breathing.
The health worker said to the mother, "When Maya has diarrhoea, is there any blood in the stool?" The mother said, "No."

The health worker checked for signs of dehydration. Maya is not lethargic or unconscious. She is not restless or irritable. Her eyes are not sunken. Maya drinks eagerly when offered some water. Her skin pinch goes back immediately.
Record Maya's signs and classify them.
learningPoints: Maya has only one sign of dehydration: she drinks eagerly.
Two signs are needed to classify SOME DEHYDRATION, so Maya has NO DEHYDRATION.
4 days is less than 14 days and there is no blood, so there is no persistent diarrhoea and no dysentery.
exercises.explain: Maya has only one sign of dehydration: she drinks eagerly. Two signs are needed to classify SOME DEHYDRATION, so Maya has NO DEHYDRATION. 4 days is less than 14 days and there is no blood, so there is no persistent diarrhoea and no dysentery.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Exercise B (Rana, 14 months)
narrative: Rana is 14 months old. She weighs 12 kg. Her temperature is 37.5 °C. Rana's mother said the child has had diarrhoea for 3 weeks.
Rana does not have any general danger signs. She does not have cough or difficult breathing.
The health worker assessed her diarrhoea. He noted she has had diarrhoea for 21 days. He asked if there has been blood in the child's stool. The mother said, "No."
The health worker checked Rana for signs of dehydration. The child is irritable throughout the visit. Her eyes are not sunken. She drinks eagerly. The skin pinch goes back immediately.
Record Rana's signs and classify.
learningPoints: Rana is irritable and drinks eagerly: two signs in the yellow row, so SOME DEHYDRATION.
She has had diarrhoea for 21 days (14 days or more) and has dehydration, so she is also classified SEVERE PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA.
Her dehydration is treated before referral, because she has no other severe classification.
exercises.explain: Rana is irritable and drinks eagerly: two signs in the yellow row, so SOME DEHYDRATION. She has had diarrhoea for 21 days (14 days or more) and has dehydration, so she is also classified SEVERE PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA. Her dehydration is treated before referral, because she has no other severe classification.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Exercise C (classify)
narrative: Answer the questions about assessing and classifying diarrhoea and dehydration.

questions.question: How many signs are needed to classify a child with SOME DEHYDRATION?
questions.explain: Two signs from: restless and irritable; sunken eyes; drinks eagerly, thirsty; skin pinch goes back slowly.

questions.question: Which pair of signs may indicate that a child has SEVERE DEHYDRATION?
options: Lethargic, and skin pinch goes back very slowly
Restless and irritable, and drinks eagerly
Sunken eyes, and skin pinch goes back slowly
questions.explain: SEVERE DEHYDRATION needs two of: lethargic or unconscious; sunken eyes; not able to drink or drinking poorly; skin pinch goes back very slowly (longer than 2 seconds).

questions.question: What type of ORS should be used to treat dehydration?
Which children need zinc supplements?
points: Children with diarrhoea who do not need immediate referral: diarrhoea with some or no dehydration
Children with persistent diarrhoea receive zinc for 14 days
Children with dysentery also receive zinc (national booklet)
Zinc is only given from 2 months up to 5 years

questions.question: What are the 4 rules of home treatment of diarrhoea?
points: Give extra fluid: as much as the child will take
Give zinc
Continue feeding
When to return: for a follow-up visit, or immediately if danger signs develop

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Exercise D (Pano)
narrative: Pano has had diarrhoea for five days. He has no blood in the stool.
He is irritable. His eyes are sunken. His father and mother also think that Pano's eyes are sunken.
The health worker offers Pano some water, and the child drinks eagerly. When the health worker pinches the skin on the child's abdomen, it goes back slowly.
Record the child's signs and classification for dehydration on the recording form.
learningPoints: Pano is irritable, has sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, and his skin pinch goes back slowly.
These are signs in the yellow row, and he has none in the red row: SOME DEHYDRATION.
exercises.explain: Pano is irritable, has sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, and his skin pinch goes back slowly. These are signs in the yellow row, and he has none in the red row: SOME DEHYDRATION.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Exercise D (Jane)
narrative: Jane has had diarrhoea for 3 days. There was no blood in the stool.
The child was not lethargic or unconscious. She was not irritable or restless. Her eyes were sunken.
She was able to drink, but she was not thirsty. The skin pinch went back immediately.
Record the child's signs and classification for dehydration on the recording form.
learningPoints: Jane has only one sign: sunken eyes.
One sign is not enough to classify some or severe dehydration: NO DEHYDRATION.
exercises.explain: Jane has only one sign: sunken eyes. One sign is not enough to classify some or severe dehydration: NO DEHYDRATION.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Exercise E (Plan B)
narrative: Answer the questions about Plan B for dehydrated children. Use the Plan B table of the national chart booklet.

questions.question: Andras is 3 years old and has SOME DEHYDRATION. How much ORS solution is he likely to need in the first 4 hours?
Gul weighs 10 kg and has SOME DEHYDRATION. How much ORS solution in the first 4 hours?
Nirveli weighs 7.5 kg and has SOME DEHYDRATION. How much ORS solution in the first 4 hours?
Sami is 11 months old and has SOME DEHYDRATION. How much ORS solution in the first 4 hours?

Vinita is 5 months old and has diarrhoea with SOME DEHYDRATION. There is no scale at the small clinic. Vinita's mother died during childbirth, so Vinita has been taking infant formula. The grandmother has recently started giving cooked cereal as well. What should Vinita be given during the first 4 hours?
options: 400–700 ml of low osmolarity ORS solution, and also 100–200 ml of clean water
200–400 ml of low osmolarity ORS solution only
questions.explain: By age (4 months up to 12 months): 400–700 ml. This is the answer of the WHO key, which adds 100–200 ml of clean water because Vinita is not breastfed.

questions.question: What should the grandmother do if Vinita vomits during the treatment?
options: Wait 10 minutes, then give the ORS solution more slowly
Stop the ORS and go to hospital
Give the same amount again at once

questions.question: When should the health worker reassess Vinita?
options: After Vinita has been given ORS solution for 4 hours on Plan B

questions.question: When Vinita is reassessed, she has NO DEHYDRATION. What treatment plan should she be put on?
questions.explain: The grandmother takes home 2 one-litre packets of ORS and gives Vinita 50–100 ml of ORS solution after each loose stool.

questions.question: Yasmin is 9 months old and weighs 8 kg. She has SOME DEHYDRATION and the health worker chooses Plan B. She breastfeeds several times each day and eats 3 meals each day. About how much ORS solution should her mother give during the first 4 hours?
During the first 4 hours of treatment, should Yasmin eat or drink anything in addition to the ORS solution?
options: Yes: she should breastfeed whenever and as much as she wants
Yes: her 3 usual meals of rice

questions.question: After 4 hours of treatment, Yasmin is still classified SOME DEHYDRATION. What is the appropriate plan to continue?
questions.explain: Begin feeding her in the clinic, and repeat Plan B.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Exercise F (Plan A)
narrative: Answer the questions about Plan A for children with diarrhoea.

questions.question: At your clinic, what are the recommended fluids for children with diarrhoea with NO DEHYDRATION?
points: Answers will vary by clinic
ORS solution
Food-based fluids such as soup, rice water and yoghurt drinks
Clean water
More frequent breastfeeding

questions.question: Somi is a 4-year-old boy with diarrhoea. He has no general danger signs and is classified NO DEHYDRATION. He will be treated according to Plan A. What are the 4 rules of home treatment of diarrhoea?
points: Give extra fluid: as much as the child will take
Give zinc
Continue feeding
When to return: for a follow-up visit, or immediately if danger signs develop

questions.question: What fluids should the health worker tell Somi's mother to give?
options: ORS solution, food-based fluids (such as soup, rice water, yoghurt drinks) and clean water
Less fluid than usual, to slow the diarrhoea

questions.question: Kasit is a 3-month-old boy with diarrhoea. He has no general danger signs and is classified NO DEHYDRATION. He is exclusively breastfed. What should the health worker tell his mother about extra fluids?
options: Breastfeed him more frequently than usual, and after breastfeeding give ORS solution or clean water
Stop breastfeeding and give only ORS until the diarrhoea stops
Give soup and rice water as well as breast milk

questions.question: For which children with NO DEHYDRATION is it especially important to give ORS at home?
points: Children who have been treated with Plan B or Plan C during the visit
Children who cannot return to a clinic if the diarrhoea gets worse

questions.question: Kala is 6 months old with NO DEHYDRATION. How much extra fluid should her mother give after each loose stool?
Sam is 2 years old with NO DEHYDRATION. How much extra fluid after each loose stool?
Kara is 15 months old with NO DEHYDRATION. How much extra fluid after each loose stool?
Lalita is 4 years old with NO DEHYDRATION. How much extra fluid after each loose stool?

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Exercise G (treat)
narrative: Answer the questions about treatment for diarrhoea and dehydration. Use the dose tables of the national chart booklet.

questions.question: How will you give zinc to a 4-month-old infant, weight 7.3 kg, with SOME DEHYDRATION?
options: ½ of a 20 mg tablet (10 mg) once each day for 14 days
1 tablet (20 mg) once each day for 14 days
½ tablet twice each day for 5 days
questions.explain: The tablet is crushed and dissolved in breast milk, ORS or clean water. It is important to give zinc for all 14 days.

questions.question: How will you give zinc to a 37-month-old child, weight 12 kg, with NO DEHYDRATION?
options: ½ of a 20 mg tablet once each day for 14 days
1 tablet (20 mg) once each day for 14 days
1 tablet once each day until the diarrhoea stops
questions.explain: The tablet can be chewed or dissolved in fluid. It is important to give zinc for all 14 days.

questions.question: How would you treat a 9-month-old, weighing 8.3 kg, with a classification of DYSENTERY?
options: Ciprofloxacin ½ tablet (250 mg) 2 times a day for 3 days, and zinc
Ciprofloxacin 1 tablet (250 mg) 2 times a day for 3 days, and zinc
questions.explain: 4 months up to 12 months (6 kg up to 10 kg): ½ tablet. Follow up in 3 days.

questions.question: How would you treat a 36-month-old, weighing 15 kg, with a classification of DYSENTERY?
options: Ciprofloxacin ½ tablet (250 mg) 2 times a day for 3 days, and zinc
Ciprofloxacin 1 tablet (250 mg) 2 times a day for 3 days, and zinc
ORS only: no antibiotic is needed
questions.explain: 12 months up to 5 years (10 kg up to 19 kg): 1 tablet. Follow up in 3 days.

questions.question: How would you treat a 7-month-old with SEVERE PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA and no other severe classification?
options: Treat the dehydration, then refer to hospital, with the mother giving frequent sips of ORS on the way
Give special feeding advice and follow up in 5 days
questions.explain: Treat dehydration before referral unless the child has another severe classification.

questions.question: The mother of a 15-month-old child with PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA is counselled. He is no longer breastfed. He normally takes 2 feedings of cow's milk and 1 meal of family foods each day. His diet has not changed during the diarrhoea. Tick ALL the comments that are appropriate.
options: You were right to keep feeding your child during the diarrhoea. He needs food to stay strong.
Your child needs more food each day. Try to give him 3 family meals plus 2 feedings between meals.
Cow's milk is very bad for your child.
Your child may be having trouble digesting the cow's milk, and that may be the reason that the diarrhoea has lasted so long.
Give your child yoghurt instead of milk until the follow-up visit in 5 days. Or give only half the usual milk and increase the amount of family foods to make up for this.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Exercise H (Basaka)
narrative: Health worker Basaka must teach a mother to prepare ORS solution for her child with diarrhoea. The child was treated with Plan B during this visit. First Basaka explains how to mix the ORS, then he shows her how to do it. He asks the mother, "Do you understand?" The mother answers "yes". So Basaka gives her 2 ORS packets and says good-bye.

questions.question: What are the four rules of home treatment that must be explained to the mother?
points: GIVE EXTRA FLUID: explain what extra fluids to give. As the child was treated with Plan B, the mother should give ORS at home. Explain how much ORS solution to give after each loose stool
CONTINUE FEEDING: instruct her how to continue feeding during and after the diarrhoea
GIVE ZINC: explain the dose and schedule for 14 days of zinc, how to give it, and why it is given
WHEN TO RETURN: teach her the signs to bring the child back immediately

questions.question: What information did Basaka give the mother about the task?
points: How to mix ORS into water
He did not include what containers to use, the ratio of packets and water, how to give the ORS to her child, or how often to give it

questions.question: Basaka showed the mother an example.
Basaka asked the mother to practise.
How did Basaka check the mother's understanding?
options: With a yes/no question ("Do you understand?")
By watching her mix the ORS
questions.explain: This is not a checking question.

questions.question: Basaka checked the mother's understanding correctly.
questions.explain: The question does not show whether the caregiver learned.

questions.question: How would you have checked the mother's understanding?
points: With a checking question, for example: "How will you prepare the ORS for your child?"

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Exercise I (counsel)
narrative: Answer these questions about counselling a caregiver.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy has diarrhoea. He has no general danger signs and is classified NO DEHYDRATION. The health worker has taught his mother Plan A and given her 2 packets of ORS. Tick ALL the fluids the mother should encourage her son to drink as long as the diarrhoea continues.
options: Tea that the child usually drinks with meals
Fruit juice that the child usually drinks each day
Water from the water jug: the child can get water whenever he is thirsty
Yoghurt drink when the mother makes some for the family
questions.explain: All five should be ticked.

questions.question: Aviva is 11 months old and has diarrhoea with NO DEHYDRATION, no general danger signs and no other classification. She eats cereal and bits of meat, vegetables and fruit, and is still breastfed. Her mother lives far from the clinic and might not be able to come back for several days, even if the child gets worse. Should the health worker give ORS packets to take home?
options: Yes: 1 packet for each day of diarrhoea so far
questions.explain: ORS at home is especially important for a child who cannot return if the diarrhoea gets worse.

questions.question: What should Aviva's mother do if the child vomits while being fed the solution?
options: Wait 10 minutes before giving more fluid, then give the solution more slowly
Give a double amount to replace it

questions.question: How long should Aviva's mother continue giving extra fluid?
The health worker will teach Aviva's mother the signs to return immediately. What are they?
points: Drinking poorly, or not able to drink or breastfeed
Becomes sicker
Develops a fever
Blood in the stool

questions.question: Which is the best checking question after advice about increasing fluids during diarrhoea?
options: Do you remember some good fluids to give your child?
Will you be sure to give your child extra fluid?
How much fluid will you give your child?

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Exercise J (Evaristo's follow-up)
narrative: This clinic refers children with severe dehydration, because health workers cannot give IV or NG therapy. A hospital nearby can give IV therapy.

Evaristo was brought for follow-up of PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA after 5 days. He is 9 months old and weighs 6.5 kg. His temperature is 36.5 °C today. He is no longer breastfed. His mother feeds him cereal twice a day and gives him a milk formula 4 times each day. When you saw him last week, you advised his mother to give him only half his usual amount of milk, and to replace half the milk by giving extra servings of cereal with oil and vegetables or meat or fish added.

questions.question: What is your first step for reassessing Evaristo?
options: Ask: has the diarrhoea stopped? How many loose stools is he having per day?
Weigh him and send him home

questions.question: Evaristo's mother says the diarrhoea has not stopped. What do you do next?
options: Reassess him completely as on the ASSESS AND CLASSIFY chart, treat any problem that needs immediate attention, then refer him to hospital
Repeat the feeding advice and see him again in 5 days

questions.question: You find that Evaristo has no general danger signs and no cough. He has now had diarrhoea for about 3 weeks. There is no blood in the stool. He is restless and irritable. His eyes are not sunken. When you offer him water, he takes a sip but does not seem thirsty. A skin pinch goes back immediately. Evaristo is dehydrated.
questions.explain: He has only one sign (restless and irritable): NO DEHYDRATION.

questions.question: How will you treat Evaristo?
options: Refer him to hospital. He does not need any treatment before he leaves
Plan B for 4 hours, then send him home

questions.question: If your reassessment had found that Evaristo had SOME DEHYDRATION, what would you have done before referral?
options: Rehydrate him according to Plan B before referral
Refer at once with sips of ORS on the way
Give IV fluids by Plan C

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Review questions (post-test)
narrative: Now that you have finished the module, answer the same questions as before. This will show what you have learned.

Children lose valuable nutrients because they cannot eat

When a child has several episodes of diarrhoea a day
When a child has an episode of diarrhoea lasting 14 days or more, which is particularly dangerous for dehydration and malnutrition

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 4: Logbook assessment questions
narrative: You are allowed to use your chart booklet as you answer these questions. You should not use your study modules.

questions.question: Diarrhoea is an important childhood disease because:
options: It is a major killer of children worldwide
It is a nuisance because the child has to go to the toilet frequently

questions.question: Dehydration can be treated by replacement of water and salt using:
options: Low osmolarity ORS or IV fluids

questions.question: Why is dehydration a cause for serious concern?
options: It can cause shock to vital organs, and possibly death
It gives the child a headache
Dehydration is not a very serious health issue

questions.question: What is in ORS?
What signs do you assess for dehydration?
options: Blood in the stool or diarrhoea that persists for 14 days
Sunken eyes, loose skin (turgor) and lethargy

questions.question: Persistent diarrhoea can be classified as SEVERE PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA if the child:
options: Has diarrhoea for 10 days or more

questions.question: What are the 4 rules of home treatment in Plan A?
options: Give extra fluid, give oral antibiotics, give zinc, counsel for when to return
Give extra fluid, reduce feeding, keep the child warm, counsel for when to return
Give extra fluid, continue feeding, give zinc, and counsel for when to return

questions.question: An infant is 11 months of age and weighs 9.6 kg. She is classified as having SOME DEHYDRATION. How much ORS should she receive in the next 4 hours?
options: At least 400 ml, up to 700 ml
At least 200 ml, up to 960 ml
At least 800 ml, up to 960 ml
questions.explain: National booklet: 4 months up to 12 months, 6 kg up to 10 kg: 400–700 ml.

questions.question: Lily is restless, but drinks quickly when you give her water. How would you classify her dehydration?
Why is zinc important in the treatment of diarrhoea?
options: It replaces sodium, potassium and other electrolytes
It is useful only in those infants shown to be zinc-deficient

questions.question: What antibiotic should be given for dysentery?
Diarrhoea is when there is more water than normal in the stool and may occur at least 3 times per day.
Dehydration can be recognized by making a rapid stool examination.
Dysentery is when there is blood in the stool.
Diarrhoea causes death because of dehydration, that is, the loss of water and salt.
You need at least two signs to classify an infant with diarrhoea as having SOME DEHYDRATION.
You can classify a 3-month-old infant with diarrhoea as having SEVERE DEHYDRATION if she has sunken eyes and lethargy.
Persistent diarrhoea is when diarrhoea occurs for 3 months continuously.
questions.explain: 14 days or more.

questions.question: Shigella bacteria is the most common cause of blood in stool in children.
You do not need to give antibiotics for a child with watery diarrhoea.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 5: Pre-test
narrative: Before you begin studying this module, check what you know. After the module you will answer the same questions.

questions.question: Which of the following children has a fever that requires further investigation?
options: Imrana has an axillary temperature of 37 °C
Joy's mother says she has been feeling very hot for the past three days
Samuel's face is very flushed and red
questions.explain: History of fever is enough.

questions.question: What are common causes of fever that often kill children?
What would you give to children with high fever?
What is the recommended treatment for malaria?
Traci has a fever, generalized rash, runny nose and mouth ulcers. How would you classify?
options: She shows signs of local infections of the skin
She shows clinical signs of AIDS

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 5: Exercise A (assess and classify fever)
narrative: Answer the questions about assessing and classifying fever.

questions.question: All children with a fever should be classified for fever.
questions.explain: Children who have a fever AND signs of measles are also classified for measles.

questions.question: When will you do a malaria test?
options: In all children with fever or a history of fever who have no general danger sign and no stiff neck
Only when the child has a stiff neck
Only when the temperature is 38.5 °C or above
questions.explain: National booklet: test all fever cases. The WHO key says: in high risk areas, all children with fever; in low risk areas, any child without another clear cause of fever.

questions.question: Which signs indicate that a child has VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE?
options: Fever and any general danger sign, or stiff neck
Fever and a positive malaria test

questions.question: Reba has a positive P. vivax test and no general danger signs or stiff neck. Her temperature is 38 °C. How will you classify?
Reba requires oral antimalarials and paracetamol.
questions.explain: She requires oral antimalarials, but not paracetamol, because her fever is not high fever (38.5 °C or above).

questions.question: According to the WHO module, a child who lives in a LOW malaria risk area will never need a malaria test.
questions.explain: The child may need a test if there is no other clear cause of fever, or if the child travelled to a high risk area within 2 weeks. In the national booklet, all fever cases are tested.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 5: Exercise B (assess and classify measles)
narrative: Answer the questions about assessing and classifying measles.

questions.question: When should a child be classified for measles?
options: If the child has a fever and shows signs of measles now, or has had measles in the last 3 months
Only if the child has mouth ulcers

questions.question: When you assess a child with fever for measles, what signs will you look for?
points: First, a generalized rash
If the rash is present, also one of: cough, runny nose, or red eyes

questions.question: Allan has a fever and measles, with deep, extensive mouth ulcers. How will you classify?
options: MEASLES WITH EYE OR MOUTH COMPLICATIONS

questions.question: Which signs indicate that a child has MEASLES WITH EYE OR MOUTH COMPLICATIONS?
options: Signs of measles, and also pus draining from the eye or mouth ulcers
Signs of measles and red eyes
Signs of measles and clouding of the cornea

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 5: Exercise C (Kareem, 5 months)
narrative: Kareem is 5 months old. He weighs 5.2 kg. His axillary temperature is 37.5 °C. His mother said he is not eating well. She said he feels hot, and she wants a health worker to help him.
Kareem is able to drink, has not vomited, does not have convulsions, and is not lethargic or unconscious. Kareem does not have a cough, said his mother. He does not have diarrhoea.

Because Kareem's temperature is 37.5 °C and he feels hot, the health worker assessed Kareem further for signs related to fever. It is the rainy season. The mother said Kareem's fever began 2 days ago. He has not had measles within the last 3 months. He does not have stiff neck, his nose is not runny, and there are no signs suggesting measles.
He had a positive RDT test for P. falciparum.
learningPoints: Kareem has fever: his temperature is 37.5 °C and he feels hot.
He has no general danger sign and no stiff neck, so he does not have the red classification.
His malaria test is positive: MALARIA.
He has no signs of measles, so he is not classified for measles.
exercises.explain: Kareem has fever: his temperature is 37.5 °C and he feels hot. He has no general danger sign and no stiff neck, so he does not have the red classification. His malaria test is positive: MALARIA. He has no signs of measles, so he is not classified for measles.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 5: Exercise D (Dolma, 12 months)
narrative: Dolma is 12 months old. She weighs 7.2 kg. Her axillary temperature is 36.5 °C. Her mother brought Dolma to the health centre today because she feels hot.

Dolma has no general danger signs. She does not have cough or difficult breathing. When asked about diarrhoea, the mother said, "Yes, Dolma has had diarrhoea for 2 to 3 days." She has not seen any blood in the stool. Dolma has not been lethargic or unconscious. Her eyes are not sunken. She drinks normally. Her skin pinch returns immediately.

The health worker said, "You brought Dolma today because she feels hot. I will check her for fever." Her mother said that Dolma has felt hot for 2 days. She has not had measles within the last 3 months. There is no stiff neck and no runny nose.
Dolma has a dry, generalized rash. She also has red eyes. She has a negative malaria test.
learningPoints: Dolma has a history of fever (she has felt hot for 2 days), so she is assessed for fever although her temperature is 36.5 °C.
She has no general danger sign and no stiff neck, and her malaria test is negative: FEVER: NO MALARIA.

She has a generalized rash and red eyes, so she has signs of measles. With no mouth ulcers, no pus draining from the eye and no clouding of the cornea, she is also classified MEASLES and gets vitamin A.
Her diarrhoea has no signs of dehydration: NO DEHYDRATION.
exercises.explain: Dolma has a history of fever (she has felt hot for 2 days), so she is assessed for fever although her temperature is 36.5 °C. She has no general danger sign and no stiff neck, and her malaria test is negative: FEVER: NO MALARIA. She has a generalized rash and red eyes, so she has signs of measles. With no mouth ulcers, no pus draining from the eye and no clouding of the cornea, she is also classified MEASLES and gets vitamin A. Her diarrhoea has no signs of dehydration: NO DEHYDRATION.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 5: Exercise E (treat malaria)
narrative: Answer the questions about oral antimalarial treatment. Use the dose tables of the national chart booklet.

questions.question: Why are chloroquine and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) no longer the first-line and second-line antimalarial medicines in the IMNCI guidelines of many countries?
options: Resistance to chloroquine has emerged and grown, and resistance to SP is growing as well
They cannot be given to children

questions.question: What does WHO recommend for oral antimalarial treatment?
questions.explain: ACT very quickly reduces the number of malaria parasites and improves the symptoms.

questions.question: A child of 6 months weighs 10 kg and has MALARIA. How do you give artemether-lumefantrine (20/120 mg)?
options: 1 tablet now, 1 tablet after 8 hours, then 1 tablet twice a day for the next two days
2 tablets now, 2 tablets after 8 hours, then 2 tablets twice a day for the next two days
1 tablet once a day for 3 days
questions.explain: 5 kg up to 15 kg: 1 tablet per dose, 6 doses.

questions.question: A child weighs 16 kg and has MALARIA. How do you give artemether-lumefantrine (20/120 mg)?
options: 1 tablet now, 1 tablet after 8 hours, then 1 tablet twice a day for the next two days
2 tablets now, 2 tablets after 8 hours, then 2 tablets twice a day for the next two days
3 tablets once a day for 3 days
questions.explain: 15 kg up to 25 kg: 2 tablets per dose, 12 tablets in all.

questions.question: A 12 kg child needs the second-line antimalarial of the national booklet, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine. What do you give?
options: 1 tablet (40/320 mg) once daily for 3 days
1 tablet (20/160 mg) twice daily for 3 days
1½ tablets (20/160 mg) once daily for 7 days
questions.explain: 11 kg up to 18 kg: 1 tablet of 40/320 mg once daily for 3 days.

questions.question: What special instructions are given with artemether-lumefantrine?
points: Give the first dose in the clinic and observe for 1 hour
If the child vomits within the hour, repeat the dose
Give the second dose at home 8 hours later
It must be taken with food

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 5: Exercise F (counsel)
narrative: Answer the questions about counselling a caregiver about fever.

questions.question: What are the 3 basic teaching steps?
points: Give information
Demonstrate (show an example)
Ask the caregiver to practise

questions.question: What are important instructions for the caregiver about treating the eye with ointment? List 5.
points: The dose of tetracycline eye ointment is the size of a grain of rice
Treat both eyes
Wash hands before and after treating the eye
Clean the child's eyes before applying ointment, with a clean cloth
Do not touch the tube to the eye or lid
Put the ointment in the lower lid of the eye, holding the lid down
Apply 3 times a day: morning, mid-day and evening
Treat until the redness is gone
If pus remains after 2 days, return to the clinic
Do not put other drops, ointments or treatments in the eye

questions.question: When should children with FEVER: NO MALARIA return for follow-up?
options: In 3 days, if the fever persists
questions.explain: National booklet and WHO answer key: 3 days if fever persists.

questions.question: When should children with MEASLES WITH EYE OR MOUTH COMPLICATIONS return for follow-up?
options: In 4 days, if signs of measles (rash, runny nose, red eyes) persist

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 5: Exercise G (follow-up: Lin and Sindi)
narrative: In this clinic, artemether-lumefantrine (AL) is the first-line oral antimalarial and dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine is the second-line oral antimalarial.

Lin's mother has brought him back to the clinic because he still has fever. Two days ago he was given AL for MALARIA, and a dose of paracetamol. His mother says that he has no new problems, just the fever. He is 3 years old and weighs 14 kg. His axillary temperature is 38.5 °C.

questions.question: How would you reassess Lin?
options: Do a full reassessment for other causes of fever, and test again for malaria by microscopy

questions.question: When you reassess Lin, he has no general danger signs, no cough and no diarrhoea. He has now had fever for 4 days. He has no stiff neck, no runny nose and no generalized rash. The microscopy slide is positive for malaria parasites. He has no ear problem and no other apparent cause of fever. How would you treat Lin?
options: Second-line antimalarial: dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, 1 tablet (40/320 mg) once daily for 3 days, first dose in the clinic
questions.explain: 14 kg is in the band 11 kg up to 18 kg. His temperature is 38.5 °C, so he also gets a dose of paracetamol. He returns in 3 days if the fever persists. (The WHO key gives its own second-line example, artesunate plus amodiaquine.)

questions.question: Sindi's mother has come back because Sindi still has a fever. Three days ago she had a positive rapid malaria test and was given treatment for MALARIA. Her mother says she is sicker now, vomiting and very hot. Sindi is 18 months old and weighs 11 kg. Her axillary temperature is 39 °C. Yesterday she could drink, but she vomited after eating. She has not had convulsions. She will not wake up when her mother tries to wake her: she is unconscious. She has no cough or diarrhoea. She has now had fever for 5 days. She has no stiff neck, runny nose or generalized rash. How do you classify Sindi?
questions.explain: Sindi is unconscious: a general danger sign.

questions.question: How will you manage Sindi?
points: Refer URGENTLY: she has a general danger sign
Give the first dose of the antimalarial for severe malaria (IM quinine)
Give the first dose of antibiotic (IM ampicillin and gentamicin, as she is unconscious)
Give one dose of paracetamol for high fever
Treat to prevent low blood sugar: Sindi is unconscious, so give by nasogastric tube if you can

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 5: Logbook assessment questions
narrative: You are allowed to use your chart booklet as you answer these questions. You should not use your study modules.

questions.question: Which of the following signs is used in IMNCI to determine if a child has a fever?
options: She has a rectal temperature of 37.5 °C or above
She has a history of fever

questions.question: One of the possible causes of a fever is:
